pred_answer: No. Deploying an AI system that infers employees' emotions from webcam feeds during work in order to flag disengagement is a prohibited AI practice under Article 5(1)(f) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, which bans the placing on the market, putting into service or use of AI systems to infer emotions of a natural person in the area of the workplace, save where the system is intended to be put in place or into the market for medical or safety reasons. The prohibition binds the deploying company as well as the provider, since Article 5(1) covers "use", not only market placement. The system falls squarely within the definition: an "emotion recognition system" is an AI system for the purpose of identifying or inferring emotions or intentions of natural persons on the basis of their biometric data (Article 3(39)), and facial images captured by webcam are biometric data within Article 3(34). Recital 18 confirms that the notion covers inferred emotional states such as satisfaction, contempt or shame, while excluding physical states such as pain or fatigue and the mere detection of readily apparent expressions, gestures or movements unless those are used to infer emotions, here they are, since the output is an inference about engagement, an emotional/intentional state, not a physical state. Recital 44 explains the rationale: the imbalance of power in the context of work, combined with the intrusiveness and the limited reliability, specificity and generalisability of such systems, means they may lead to detrimental or unfavourable treatment of workers. The only carve-out is narrow and does not assist here. It applies where the emotion-recognition system is intended to be put in place or on the market strictly for medical or safety reasons, for example therapeutic use, or fatigue detection in pilots or drivers to prevent accidents (which Recital 18 in any event excludes from the concept of "emotion" itself). Productivity, engagement or disengagement monitoring is a workforce-management purpose, not a medical or safety purpose, and the purpose must be the system's intended purpose (Article 3(12)) at the time it is put into service; it cannot be retrofitted after the fact. Employee consent does not cure the breach: Article 5(1) admits no consent-based derogation, and in the employment context consent would in any case be unlikely to be freely given. Because the practice is prohibited, no compliance route is available and the downstream regimes are not a fallback: the system would otherwise be high-risk both as an emotion-recognition system under Annex III, point 1(c) and as a system used to monitor and evaluate the performance and behaviour of persons in work-related relationships under Annex III, point 4(b), attracting the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements including the Article 9 risk-management system, Article 10 data governance, Article 13 instructions for use, Article 14 human oversight, Article 49 registration, and the deployer's Article 50(3) duty to inform exposed persons of the system's operation and to process personal data in accordance with Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (that Article 50(3) duty being disapplied only for biometric categorisation and emotion recognition permitted by law to detect, prevent or investigate criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards). Those obligations would only ever become relevant to a differently-designed system that genuinely sits outside Article 5(1)(f), for instance a safety-purpose fatigue-detection system. The described deployment must not be put into service, and it must be discontinued if already running.

This practice is prohibited by Article 5(1)(g) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. That point bans the placing on the market, the putting into service for this specific purpose, or the use of biometric categorisation systems that categorise individually natural persons on the basis of their biometric data to deduce or infer their race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation. Facial images are biometric data within Article 3(34), and a system assigning natural persons to categories on that basis is a biometric categorisation system within Article 3(40); race, political opinions and sexual orientation are three of the listed sensitive attributes, so a single inferred attribute would already suffice. Two qualifiers bound the prohibition. First, Article 5(1)(g) does not cover the labelling or filtering of lawfully acquired biometric datasets, such as images, based on biometric data, nor the categorising of biometric data in the area of law enforcement, a carve-out that reaches sorting by readily observable features (Recital 30 gives hair or eye colour as examples), not the deduction of race, political opinions or sexual orientation described here. Second, the Article 3(40) definition itself excludes categorisation that is ancillary to another commercial service and strictly necessary for objective technical reasons; inferring these attributes as the system's stated output is not ancillary in that sense. The prohibition binds providers and deployers alike and applies under Article 2(1) to providers placing the system on the Union market irrespective of their place of establishment, to deployers established in the Union, and to providers and deployers in third countries where the output is used in the Union. Because the practice falls under Article 5, no high-risk classification analysis under Article 6(2) and Annex III point 1(b) arises and the Article 50(3) deployer information duty cannot cure it: the practice is banned outright rather than permitted subject to conditions.

Yes. Building a facial-recognition database in that way is a prohibited AI practice under Article 5(1)(e). Article 5(1)(e) prohibits the placing on the market, the putting into service for this specific purpose, or the use of AI systems that create or expand facial recognition databases through the untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV footage. The vendor's conduct matches each element: the system creates (and, as it is fed further material, expands) a facial recognition database; the collection is indiscriminate, which is precisely the "untargeted" scraping the provision targets; and both named sources, the internet and CCTV footage, are covered, so it is immaterial which of the two supplies the bulk of the images. The prohibition attaches to the vendor as the entity placing the system on the market and putting it into service, and equally to anyone who subsequently uses it. Article 5(1)(e) carries no internal limbs, conditions or carve-outs. Unlike the biometric categorisation prohibition in Article 5(1)(g), which expressly does not cover the labelling or filtering of lawfully acquired biometric datasets or the categorising of biometric data in the area of law enforcement, and unlike Article 5(1)(h), whose prohibition on 'real-time' remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement is qualified by the objectives in points (i) to (iii) and the safeguards in Article 5(2) to (5), point (e) admits no exception for law enforcement, security, research or consent-based justifications. Nor can the practice be rehabilitated by treating the system as a high-risk remote biometric identification system under Annex III, point 1(a): Article 5 operates as an outright ban, so the Article 6(2) route and the Article 6(3) derogation conditions are never reached. By virtue of Article 5(8), the prohibition is also without prejudice to prohibitions applying where the practice infringes other Union law, so compliance analysis under Union data protection law runs in parallel rather than displacing Article 5(1)(e).

Yes. An AI app that targets elderly users with cognitive decline and leverages that condition to steer them into expensive subscriptions falls within the prohibition in Article 5(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, which bans the placing on the market, the putting into service or the use of an AI system that exploits any of the vulnerabilities of a natural person or a specific group of persons due to their age, disability or a specific social or economic situation, with the objective, or the effect, of materially distorting the behaviour of that person or a person belonging to that group in a manner that causes or is reasonably likely to cause that person or another person significant harm. Each limb is satisfied on the facts described. The targeted group is defined by age and by a cognitive impairment, so the vulnerability ground is met on both the "age" and "disability" alternatives; the design intentionally leverages that impairment, which is exploitation rather than mere incidental effect; and pushing users toward purchases they would not otherwise make is material distortion of behaviour. The one element that must still be established on the facts is significant harm, the prohibition requires that the distorted behaviour causes, or is reasonably likely to cause, significant harm to that person or another person, so the recurring financial detriment (subscription cost relative to the user's means, duration of the commitment, difficulty of cancellation, cumulative depletion of savings) must reach that threshold. Note that intent is not required: the "objective, or the effect" wording means an operator cannot escape Article 5(1)(b) by disclaiming a deliberate aim where the exploitative effect is present. Article 5(1)(a) is an independent and cumulative ground on the same facts: if the app deploys subliminal techniques beyond a person's consciousness or purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques, dark patterns, false urgency, concealed pricing or renewal terms, with the objective or effect of materially distorting behaviour by appreciably impairing the ability to make an informed decision, thereby causing a decision the person would not otherwise have taken, and causing or being reasonably likely to cause significant harm, that limb is breached in addition to point (b). Neither prohibition depends on the system being classified as high-risk under Article 6, and neither is subject to any authorisation or derogation of the kind Article 5(2) to (4) provides for real-time remote biometric identification under Article 5(1)(h). The prohibition binds the full operator chain, placing on the market, putting into service and use, so both the provider and any deployer are caught, and under Article 2(1) it applies to providers placing the system on the Union market irrespective of their place of establishment, to deployers established in the Union, and to providers and deployers in third countries where the output is used in the Union. The exclusions in Article 2 do not assist: only genuine pre-market research, testing or development activity is carved out by Article 2(8), and testing in real world conditions is expressly not covered. Article 2(7) preserves the parallel application of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 and the other data-protection instruments, and Article 2(5) leaves Chapter II of Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 unaffected, so consumer-protection and data-protection exposure runs alongside the AI Act breach. Enforcement follows Article 79: a market surveillance authority with sufficient reason to consider that the system presents a risk to health, safety or fundamental rights evaluates it and, on finding non-compliance, requires the operator to withdraw the system from the Union market, recall it from the distribution chain or restrict its availability within a prescribed period proportionate to the risk.

Indiscriminate real-time remote facial identification of all passers-by in a city square is prohibited. Article 5(1)(h) bans the use of "real-time" remote biometric identification systems in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes, and a city square is a "publicly accessible space" within Article 3(44), any publicly or privately owned physical place accessible to an undetermined number of natural persons. Scanning everyone who passes is by definition untargeted, so it cannot satisfy the prohibition's exhaustive derogations, each of which requires that use be strictly necessary for one of three objectives: (i) the targeted search for specific victims of abduction, trafficking in human beings or sexual exploitation of human beings, and the search for missing persons; (ii) the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to the life or physical safety of natural persons, or of a genuine and present or genuine and foreseeable threat of a terrorist attack; and (iii) the localisation or identification of a person suspected of having committed a criminal offence, for a criminal investigation, prosecution or execution of a criminal penalty, for offences listed in Annex II (terrorism; trafficking in human beings; sexual exploitation of children and child pornography; illicit trafficking in narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances; illicit trafficking in weapons, munitions or explosives; murder and grievous bodily injury; illicit trade in human organs or tissue; illicit trafficking in nuclear or radioactive materials; kidnapping, illegal restraint or hostage-taking; crimes within the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court; unlawful seizure of aircraft or ships; rape; environmental crime; organised or armed robbery; sabotage; participation in a criminal organisation involved in those offences), punishable in the Member State concerned by a custodial sentence or detention order for a maximum period of at least four years. Point (h) is without prejudice to Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 for processing of biometric data for non-law-enforcement purposes. Even a genuinely targeted operation is lawful only under the layered conditions of Article 5(2), (5): the deploying authority must take account of the nature of the situation giving rise to the possible use, in particular the seriousness, probability and scale of the harm avoided, and of the consequences for the rights and freedoms of all persons concerned; the use must comply with necessary and proportionate safeguards and conditions in the authorising national law, in particular temporal, geographic and personal limitations; the law-enforcement authority must have completed a fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27 and registered the system in the EU database under Article 49; each use must be authorised in advance by a judicial or independent administrative authority under Article 5(3); uses must be notified to the relevant market surveillance and national data protection authorities under Article 5(4); and, under Article 5(5), the derogations operate only if the Member State has enabled them in national law, which may be more restrictive. Where such use is lawfully permitted, the system is high-risk as a remote biometric identification system under Annex III, point 1(a) and Article 6(2), triggering provider duties under Article 16, conformity assessment under Article 43(1) (Annex VI internal control where harmonised standards or common specifications are applied, otherwise Annex VII, with the market surveillance authority acting as notified body for law-enforcement deployments), registration in the secure non-public section of the EU database under Article 49(4), deployer duties under Article 26 (use per the instructions, competent and trained human oversight, monitoring and serious-incident reporting, and retention of automatically generated logs for at least six months), and human oversight under Article 14, including the Article 14(5) rule that no action or decision may be taken on an identification unless separately verified and confirmed by at least two competent natural persons, a requirement that does not apply to law-enforcement, migration, border-control or asylum use where Union or national law considers it disproportionate.

The system is high-risk. An AI system intended to be used as a safety component in the management and operation of the supply of electricity falls squarely within the critical infrastructure area of Annex III, point 2, which covers safety components in the management and operation of critical digital infrastructure, road traffic, or the supply of water, gas, heating or electricity. Classification therefore follows the Annex III listed-use route in Article 6(2), under which AI systems referred to in Annex III shall be considered high-risk, not the Annex I product route in Article 6(1), which requires both that the system be a safety component of (or itself be) a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that that product undergo third-party conformity assessment under that legislation. The derogation in Article 6(3) is in principle available but will not realistically apply here: it exempts an Annex III system only where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision-making, and only where one of four conditions is met, the system performs a narrow procedural task; it improves the result of a previously completed human activity; it detects decision-making patterns or deviations from prior patterns and is not meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment without proper human review; or it performs a preparatory task to an assessment relevant to an Annex III use case. A system performing a genuine grid-safety function materially influences operational outcomes and so meets none of these; in any event, a system that performs profiling of natural persons is always high-risk notwithstanding those conditions. A provider that nonetheless considers the system not high-risk must document that assessment before placing it on the market or putting it into service, is subject to the registration obligation in Article 49(2), and must supply the documentation to national competent authorities on request (Article 6(4)).

Before placing a high-risk AI system on the market, importers must verify that the provider has carried out the conformity assessment, drawn up the technical documentation, and affixed the CE marking, that the system is accompanied by the EU declaration of conformity and instructions for use and that an authorised representative has been appointed (Article 22), and must indicate their identity on the system and ensure that storage and transport conditions do not jeopardise its compliance. Providers of high-risk AI systems must ensure the system meets the Chapter III Section 2 requirements and bears their identity, operate a quality-management system (Article 17), keep the technical documentation (Articles 11 and 18) and automatically generated logs (Article 19), have the system undergo conformity assessment (Article 43 requires providers of high-risk AI to undergo a conformity assessment: internal-control.), draw up the EU declaration of conformity (Article 47), affix the CE marking (Article 48), register the system in the EU database (Article 49), take corrective action where it is not in conformity (Article 20), and demonstrate compliance to competent authorities on request (Article 21).

Article 15 imposes a single design-and-development duty with three limbs and one disclosure duty. Under Article 15(1), a high-risk AI system must be designed and developed so as to achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, and to perform consistently in those respects throughout its lifecycle; the benchmark is proportionate, not absolute, and it is a continuing lifecycle obligation rather than a one-off pre-market test. Article 15(2) addresses the technical measurement of these aspects by tasking the Commission, in cooperation with relevant stakeholders and organisations such as metrology and benchmarking authorities, with encouraging the development of benchmarks and measurement methodologies, it does not itself create a provider duty. On accuracy, Article 15(3) requires the levels of accuracy and the relevant accuracy metrics to be declared in the accompanying instructions for use. That declaration is reinforced by Article 13(3)(b)(ii), under which the instructions must state the level of accuracy, including its metrics, robustness and cybersecurity referred to in Article 15 against which the system has been tested and validated and which can be expected, together with any known and foreseeable circumstances that may have an impact on that expected level; this sits within the broader Article 13(1) duty to make operation sufficiently transparent for deployers to interpret the output and use it appropriately. On robustness, Article 15(4) requires the system to be as resilient as possible regarding errors, faults or inconsistencies that may occur within the system or the environment in which it operates, in particular due to interaction with natural persons or other systems. Robustness may be achieved through technical redundancy solutions, which may include backup or fail-safe plans. Article 15(4) further requires that high-risk AI systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market or put into service be developed in such a way as to eliminate or reduce as far as possible the risk of possibly biased outputs influencing input for future operations, and to ensure that any such feedback loops are duly addressed with appropriate mitigation measures. On cybersecurity, Article 15(5) requires resilience against attempts by unauthorised third parties to alter the system's use, outputs or performance by exploiting system vulnerabilities. The technical solutions must be appropriate to the relevant circumstances and the risks, and the solutions addressing AI-specific vulnerabilities must include, where appropriate, measures to prevent, detect, respond to, resolve and control for attacks manipulating the training data set (data poisoning), attacks on pre-trained components used in training (model poisoning), inputs designed to cause the model to make a mistake (adversarial examples or model evasion), confidentiality attacks, and model flaws. Two related points bear on compliance. Data quality feeds the accuracy requirement: Article 10(3) requires training, validation and testing data sets to be relevant, sufficiently representative and, to the best extent possible, free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose, and Article 10(4) requires them to reflect the specific geographical, contextual, behavioural or functional setting of intended use. And under Article 42(2), a high-risk AI system certified, or for which a statement of conformity has been issued, under a cybersecurity scheme pursuant to Regulation (EU) 2019/881 whose references have been published in the Official Journal is presumed to comply with the cybersecurity requirements of Article 15, but only in so far as that certificate or statement, or parts of it, cover those requirements.

Yes. A provider must register itself and the system in the EU database before the system is put into service, and the governing provision is Article 49(1), reinforced by the provider obligation in Article 16(1)(i). Article 49(1) requires that, before placing on the market or putting into service a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III, the provider or, where applicable, the authorised representative register themselves and their system in the EU database referred to in Article 71. "Stand-alone" high-risk systems are precisely the Annex III route under Article 6(2), systems that are not safety components of, or themselves, products covered by the Annex I harmonisation legislation under Article 6(1). Registration is therefore a pre-service condition, not a post-deployment formality, and Article 71(2) makes the provider (or authorised representative) responsible for entering the data listed in Sections A and B of Annex VIII into that database. Three qualifications complete the duty. First, the exception in Article 49(1) itself: high-risk systems referred to in point 2 of Annex III (critical infrastructure) are excluded from EU-database registration and are instead registered at national level under Article 49(5). Second, where the provider has concluded under Article 6(3) that an Annex III system is not high-risk, registration is still owed, Article 49(2) requires that provider or authorised representative to register themselves and that system in the EU database before placing on the market or putting into service, and Article 6(4) confirms that the self-assessment must be documented beforehand and that the Article 49(2) registration obligation applies. Third, where the provider is established outside the Union, Article 22(3)(e) makes compliance with the registration obligations part of the mandate the authorised representative must be empowered to carry out, and Article 22(1) requires that representative to be appointed before the system is made available on the Union market. Registration sits alongside, and does not substitute for, the other pre-service steps in Article 16(1): conformity assessment under Article 43 prior to placing on the market or putting into service (point (f)), the EU declaration of conformity under Article 47 (point (g)), and affixing the CE marking under Article 48 (point (h)).

The system is high-risk. It falls under Article 6(2) read with Annex III, point 7(d), which lists AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of competent public authorities, or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies, in the context of migration, asylum or border control management for the purpose of detecting, recognising or identifying natural persons, subject only to the carve-out for the verification of travel documents. Biometric identification of the traveller himself is not the verification of a travel document, so the carve-out does not remove it; the area heading also applies only in so far as the use is permitted under relevant Union or national law, and a border authority operating migration control satisfies the actor condition (whether run in-house or by a contractor acting on its behalf). It is immaterial that Annex III, point 1(a) excludes from the biometrics area those systems used for biometric verification whose sole purpose is to confirm that a person is who he claims to be: that exclusion operates within point 1 only and does not limit point 7(d), which covers recognition and identification in the border-control context on its own terms. If instead the system merely authenticates the chip or the security features of the passport or visa, it would fall in the travel-document exception and not be high-risk on that limb. The Article 6(3) derogation is unlikely to rescue it: it applies only where the system poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights and is limited to a narrow procedural task, to improving the result of a previously completed human activity, to detecting decision-making patterns or deviations from prior patterns without replacing or influencing the human assessment, or to a preparatory task to an assessment, and it never applies where the system performs profiling of natural persons. A system that itself establishes identity at the border determines the outcome rather than preparing it, and a provider relying on the derogation must document that assessment before placing the system on the market or putting it into service (Article 6(4)). Consequently the provider bears the Article 16 obligations: compliance with the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements; indication of its name, registered trade name or trade mark and contact address on the system, its packaging or accompanying documentation; a quality management system under Article 17 (covering the regulatory-compliance strategy, design control and design verification, development and quality assurance, examination, test and validation procedures, technical specifications, data management, the Article 9 risk management system, post-market monitoring, serious-incident reporting, communication with authorities, record-keeping, resource management and an accountability framework); retention of the Article 18 documentation and of the Article 11 technical documentation with the Annex IV content; retention, when under its control, of the automatically generated logs under Article 19 for a period appropriate to the intended purpose and at least six months; conformity assessment under Article 43 before placing on the market or putting into service; the written, machine-readable, signed and dated EU declaration of conformity under Article 47 with the Annex V content, kept at the disposal of national competent authorities for 10 years and translated as required; CE marking under Article 48; registration under Article 49(1); corrective action under Article 20; accessibility in accordance with Directives (EU) 2016/2102 and (EU) 2019/882; and demonstration of compliance to a national competent authority upon reasoned request. Because the system sits in point 7 of Annex III, registration under Article 49 takes the restricted form in Article 49(4): the provider's (and, where the deployer is a public authority, the deployer's) registration is made in a secure non-public section of the EU database referred to in Article 71, and is limited to Annex VIII Section A, points 1 to 10 excluding points 6, 8 and 9; Annex VIII Section B, points 1 to 5 and points 8 and 9; Annex VIII Section C, points 1 to 3; and points 1, 2, 3 and 5 of Annex IX, with access confined to the Commission and the national authorities referred to in Article 74(8). A provider established outside the Union must, before placing the system on the market, appoint by written mandate an authorised representative in the Union (Article 22), whose mandate must empower it to verify that the Article 47 declaration and Article 11 technical documentation were drawn up and an appropriate conformity assessment carried out, to keep the provider's contact details, the declaration, the technical documentation and any notified-body certificate available to competent authorities for 10 years, to provide that documentation on reasoned request, to cooperate with competent authorities, and to comply with applicable registration obligations; the representative must terminate the mandate and inform the AI Office and the relevant market surveillance authority where it has reason to believe the provider acts contrary to its obligations. Distributors must, before making the system available, verify the CE marking, the accompanying EU declaration of conformity and instructions for use, and the provider's and importer's compliance with Article 16, points (b) and (c) and Article 23(3); withhold the system where they consider it non-conforming until it is brought into conformity; and inform the provider or importer, and the relevant authorities, where the system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1).

Before first use the authority must carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment (FRIA) under Article 27(1). The system described, an AI system used by a public authority to evaluate natural persons' eligibility for essential public assistance benefits and services, or to grant, reduce, revoke or reclaim such benefits, is high-risk under Article 6(2) by virtue of Annex III, point 5(a), and the deployer is a body governed by public law, so it falls squarely within Article 27(1); the sole carve-out in that paragraph, for systems intended to be used in the area listed in point 2 of Annex III (critical infrastructure), does not apply. The assessment must consist of all six elements listed in Article 27(1): (a) a description of the deployer's processes in which the high-risk AI system will be used in line with its intended purpose; (b) a description of the period of time within which, and the frequency with which, the system is intended to be used; (c) the categories of natural persons and groups likely to be affected by its use in the specific context; (d) the specific risks of harm likely to have an impact on those categories, taking into account the information given by the provider under Article 13; (e) a description of the implementation of human oversight measures, according to the instructions for use; and (f) the measures to be taken if those risks materialise, including the arrangements for internal governance and complaint mechanisms. Under Article 27(2) the obligation attaches to the first use of the system; in similar cases the deployer may rely on previously conducted fundamental rights impact assessments or on existing impact assessments carried out by the provider, and if during use any of the Article 27(1) elements has changed or is no longer up to date, the deployer must take the necessary steps to update the information. Once the assessment has been performed, the deployer must notify the market surveillance authority of its results, submitting the filled-out template referred to in Article 27(5), which the AI Office is to develop (Article 27(3)); where any of these obligations is already met through a data protection impact assessment, the FRIA complements that assessment (Article 27(4)). Separately, and also before putting the system into service or using it, the authority must register itself, select the system and register its use in the EU database referred to in Article 71, as required of public-authority deployers of Annex III systems by Article 49(3), again with the exception, inapplicable here, for systems listed in point 2 of Annex III.

As the deployer of the AI system that generated or manipulated the video, the media company must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated (Article 50(4), first subparagraph). That disclosure must be made to the natural persons concerned in a clear and distinguishable manner, at the latest at the time of the first exposure, and must conform to the applicable accessibility requirements (Article 50(5)). Two qualifications attach to that duty. The obligation does not apply where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences (Article 50(4), second subparagraph). And where the deepfake forms part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work or programme, a satirical treatment of the public figure, for instance, the duty is reduced to disclosing the existence of the generated or manipulated content in an appropriate manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work (Article 50(4), third subparagraph). Importantly for a publisher, the editorial-responsibility carve-out in the fourth subparagraph of Article 50(4) is confined to AI-generated or manipulated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest; human review, editorial control and the assumption of editorial responsibility do not excuse the labelling of a deepfake video. Separately, if the media company also acts as the provider of the AI system generating the synthetic video, it must ensure the outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated, using technical solutions that are effective, interoperable, robust and reliable so far as technically feasible (Article 50(2)); that marking duty does not apply to the extent the system performs an assistive function for standard editing or does not substantially alter the input data or its semantics. These transparency duties are without prejudice to the requirements of Chapter III and to other transparency obligations under Union or national law (Article 50(6)).

Both the audio and the text must be marked at source by the provider in a machine-readable format and be detectable as artificially generated or manipulated (Article 50(2)). The marking solutions must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as is technically feasible, taking into account the specificities and limitations of the various types of content, the costs of implementation and the generally acknowledged state of the art, as may be reflected in relevant technical standards. This provider duty applies to any AI system, including a general-purpose AI system, generating synthetic audio, image, video or text content, and it does not apply to the extent the system performs an assistive function for standard editing or does not substantially alter the input data provided by the deployer or the semantics thereof, or where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences (Article 50(2)). Marking under Article 50(2) does not exhaust the position where the content is published online, because separate disclosure duties fall on the deployer. If the generated or manipulated audio constitutes a deep fake, the deployer must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated; that duty does not apply where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, and where the content forms part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work or programme the duty is limited to disclosing the existence of such generated or manipulated content in an appropriate manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work (Article 50(4)). If the generated or manipulated text is published with the purpose of informing the public on matters of public interest, the deployer must disclose that the text has been artificially generated or manipulated; that text duty does not apply where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, or where the AI-generated content has undergone a process of human review or editorial control and a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility for the publication (Article 50(4)). Text published online that does not serve to inform the public on matters of public interest therefore attracts no deployer disclosure duty, but the provider's machine-readable marking duty under Article 50(2) still applies. The information owed under these paragraphs must be provided to the natural persons concerned in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of the first interaction or exposure (Article 50(5)).

Article 10 makes dataset quality a condition of lawful development: where a high-risk AI system uses techniques involving the training of AI models with data, it must be developed on the basis of training, validation and testing data sets meeting the quality criteria in paragraphs 2 to 5 whenever such data sets are used (Article 10(1)). Those data sets must be subject to data governance and management practices appropriate to the intended purpose of the system (Article 10(2)), concerning in particular: the relevant design choices; data collection processes and the origin of the data, and, for personal data, the original purpose of collection; relevant data-preparation processing operations such as annotation, labelling, cleaning, updating, enrichment and aggregation; the formulation of assumptions, in particular as to what the data are supposed to measure and represent; an assessment of the availability, quantity and suitability of the data sets needed; examination in view of possible biases likely to affect health and safety, negatively impact fundamental rights or lead to discrimination prohibited under Union law, especially where outputs influence inputs for future operations; appropriate measures to detect, prevent and mitigate biases so identified; and identification of relevant data gaps or shortcomings preventing compliance with the Regulation, together with how they can be addressed (Article 10(2)(a), (h)). Substantively, the data sets must be relevant, sufficiently representative and, to the best extent possible, free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose; they must have appropriate statistical properties, including, where applicable, as regards the persons or groups of persons in relation to whom the system is intended to be used. These characteristics may be met at the level of individual data sets or of a combination of them (Article 10(3)). The data sets must also take into account, to the extent required by the intended purpose, the characteristics or elements particular to the specific geographical, contextual, behavioural or functional setting of intended use (Article 10(4)). By way of exception, providers may process special categories of personal data where strictly necessary to ensure bias detection and correction under Article 10(2)(f) and (g), subject to appropriate safeguards for fundamental rights and freedoms and, in addition to Regulations (EU) 2016/679 and (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680, to all of the following cumulative conditions: the bias detection and correction cannot be effectively fulfilled by processing other data, including synthetic or anonymised data; the data are subject to technical limitations on re-use and to state-of-the-art security and privacy-preserving measures, including pseudonymisation; the data are subject to measures ensuring they are secured and protected with suitable safeguards, including strict controls and documentation of access, so that only authorised persons bound by confidentiality obligations have access; the data are not transmitted, transferred or otherwise accessed by other parties; the data are deleted once the bias has been corrected or the retention period ends, whichever comes first; and the records of processing activities state why the processing was strictly necessary to detect and correct biases and why that objective could not be achieved by processing other data (Article 10(5)(a), (f)). Finally, for high-risk AI systems developed without techniques involving the training of AI models, paragraphs 2 to 5 apply only to the testing data sets (Article 10(6)).

The only affirmative disclosure the Act imposes on a retail customer-support chatbot is the Article 50(1) transparency duty: the provider must design and develop the system so that the natural persons interacting with it are informed that they are interacting with an AI system. That duty is subject to two limbs. First, it does not apply where this is obvious from the point of view of a natural person who is reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect, taking into account the circumstances and the context of use, so an interface that is unmistakably labelled as a bot already satisfies the rule, though a chatbot presented under a human persona does not. Second, it does not apply to AI systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards for the rights and freedoms of third parties and unless the system is available for the public to report a criminal offence, a derogation of no use to a retailer. The manner and timing are fixed by Article 50(5): the information must be provided to the natural person concerned in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of the first interaction or exposure, and must conform with the applicable accessibility requirements. Nothing more need be disclosed, the Act does not require the retailer to name the model, explain its logic, or offer a human alternative under this provision. Two adjacent points complete the picture. If the chatbot generates synthetic audio, image, video or text content, Article 50(2) additionally obliges the provider to mark the outputs in a machine-readable format and make them detectable as artificially generated or manipulated, with the technical solution being effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as technically feasible; that duty does not apply where the system performs an assistive function for standard editing or does not substantially alter the input data. Separately, Article 4 requires the retailer, as provider or deployer, to take measures to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy of its staff and other persons operating the system on its behalf, an internal competence duty, not a disclosure to customers. A customer-support chatbot is not high-risk: it is neither a safety component of, nor itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I requiring third-party conformity assessment (Article 6(1)(a) and (b)), nor does it fall within any lettered use-case under the eight areas of Annex III (Article 6(2)). Consequently none of the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements, the Article 43 conformity assessment and CE marking, or registration in the EU database under Article 71 apply, and no Article 6(3) derogation analysis is needed. The transparency obligations in Article 50 apply from 2 August 2026; the Article 4 AI-literacy obligation applied from 2 February 2025.

The deployer's core duty is the Article 50(3) transparency obligation: it must inform the natural persons exposed to the emotion-recognition system of the operation of that system, and must process their personal data in accordance with Regulations (EU) 2016/679 and (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680, as applicable. That information must be given in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of the first interaction or exposure, and must conform to the applicable accessibility requirements (Article 50(5)). The single carve-out from Article 50(3), systems permitted by law to detect, prevent or investigate criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards, has no application to commercial market research, so the focus-group participants must be told before or at the moment they are first exposed. Article 50(6) confirms this duty is without prejudice to the Chapter III requirements and to other Union or national transparency obligations. Because emotion recognition is a listed Annex III use-case (Annex III, point 1(c)) and this use is outside the workplace and education contexts where such systems are prohibited, the system is high-risk under Article 6(2), so the Article 26 deployer obligations apply in parallel, Article 26(11) expressly preserves the Article 50 duty on top of them. The deployer must therefore take appropriate technical and organisational measures to use the system in accordance with the instructions for use (Article 26(1)); assign human oversight to natural persons with the necessary competence, training, authority and support (Article 26(2)); ensure input data is relevant and sufficiently representative for the intended purpose to the extent it controls that data (Article 26(4)); monitor operation on the basis of the instructions for use, and where it considers use in accordance with those instructions may present a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), inform the provider or distributor and the market surveillance authority without undue delay and suspend use, and immediately report any serious incident first to the provider and then to the importer or distributor and the market surveillance authorities (Article 26(5)); keep the automatically generated logs, to the extent they are under its control, for at least six months unless Union or national law provides otherwise (Article 26(6)); use the Article 13 information to carry out any data protection impact assessment required under Article 35 GDPR (Article 26(9)); and cooperate with the relevant competent authorities (Article 26(12)). The worker-information duty in Article 26(7) is not engaged, since the participants are focus-group subjects rather than workers of the deployer, and the Article 26(10) judicial-authorisation requirement is confined to post-remote biometric identification.

A corporate email spam filter that sorts incoming mail into junk and inbox folders is not high-risk under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689; it is an unregulated (minimal-risk) AI system subject only to the Article 4 AI-literacy duty, and the Chapter III provider and deployer obligations (Articles 16 to 21, 26) do not attach to it. Classification runs through the two routes in Article 6, which must be tested separately. Under the Annex I product route (Article 6(1)), the system is high-risk only if it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation; email filtering is not a safety component of machinery, radio equipment, medical devices, lifts, vehicles or any other Annex I product, so this route is not engaged. Under the Annex III route (Article 6(2)), the system must fall within a lettered use-case under one of the eight areas, biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and workers' management, access to essential private and public services, law enforcement, migration/asylum/border control, and administration of justice and democratic processes. Routing messages by content matches none of them. In particular, Annex III, point 4 is not met: the filter is not used for recruitment or selection (point 4(a)), nor to make decisions affecting terms of work-related relationships, promotion or termination, to allocate tasks based on individual behaviour or personal traits, or to monitor and evaluate the performance and behaviour of workers (point 4(b)), it classifies inbound messages, not persons. Because no Annex III use-case is engaged at all, the Article 6(3) derogation (narrow procedural task, improving a completed human activity, detecting decision-making patterns or deviations, or a preparatory task, with the profiling carve-back that always restores high-risk status) is never reached, and the associated documented self-assessment and Article 49(2) registration obligation do not arise. No transparency obligation under Article 50 is triggered either: the filter does not generate synthetic audio, image, video or text content requiring machine-readable marking (Article 50(2)), and it does not interact with natural persons as a conversational system. Two conditions would change this. If the deployer modifies the intended purpose so that the system is used to monitor and evaluate the behaviour of workers or to inform decisions on their work-related relationships, it becomes high-risk under Annex III, point 4(b), and the modifying actor is deemed a provider bearing the full Article 16 obligations (Article 25(1)(c)); the same follows from putting one's name or trademark on a high-risk system (Article 25(1)(a)) or making a substantial modification to one (Article 25(1)(b)). Separately, processing of email content remains subject to Union data-protection law, which the AI Act leaves unaffected.

A warehouse AI system used to forecast inventory demand and trigger stock re-ordering is not subject to any risk-based classification under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689: it is neither a prohibited practice nor a high-risk AI system, and it attracts no transparency duty on these facts. None of the eight practices prohibited by Article 5(1) is engaged: the system applies no subliminal, manipulative or deceptive technique and exploits no vulnerability of age, disability or socio-economic situation (Article 5(1)(a) and (b)); it performs no social scoring leading to detrimental treatment in unrelated social contexts or disproportionate to social behaviour (Article 5(1)(c)(i) and (ii)); it makes no criminal-offence risk assessment of natural persons based solely on profiling or personality traits (Article 5(1)(d)); and it involves no untargeted facial-image scraping, emotion inference in the workplace, biometric categorisation or real-time remote biometric identification for law enforcement (Article 5(1)(e) to (h)). Neither high-risk route in Article 6 is satisfied. Under the product route, the system is not a safety component of, nor itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and it is not subject to third-party conformity assessment under that legislation, so Article 6(1)(a) and (b) are not met. Under the listed-use route, demand forecasting and automated replenishment of warehouse stock falls within none of the eight areas of Annex III: biometrics (point 1), critical infrastructure as a safety component in the management or operation of critical digital infrastructure, road traffic or the supply of water, gas, heating or electricity (point 2), education and vocational training (point 3), employment and workers' management (point 4), access to and enjoyment of essential private and public services and benefits (point 5), law enforcement (point 6), migration, asylum and border control management (point 7), or administration of justice and democratic processes (point 8). Because Annex III is not triggered, the Article 6(3) derogation and its conditions in points (a) to (d), narrow procedural task, improving a previously completed human activity, detecting decision-making patterns or deviations, or a preparatory task, do not need to be tested, and the counter-rule that an Annex III system performing profiling of natural persons is always high-risk is likewise not reached; ordinary commercial logistics management is simply outside the list. Article 50 imposes no duty here either, provided the tool remains an internal forecasting and ordering system: the Article 50(1) disclosure duty applies only to AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons, and even then not where the AI nature is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person; the marking duty in Article 50(2) concerns providers of systems generating synthetic audio, image, video or text content; and the duties in Article 50(3) and (4) bind deployers of emotion recognition or biometric categorisation systems and of deep fakes or AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest. If the tool were extended with a user-facing conversational interface, the Article 50(1) information would have to be given clearly and distinguishably at the latest at the time of the first interaction and in conformity with applicable accessibility requirements (Article 50(5)). The system therefore sits in the minimal-risk tier, where the Regulation imposes no product-compliance requirements; the operator remains free to apply voluntary measures, and the classification would need revisiting only if the system's intended purpose changed, for example if it were repurposed as a safety component in the management or operation of one of the critical infrastructures in Annex III, point 2, or applied to decisions about workers within Annex III, point 4.

No, a spelling and grammar checker in a word processor triggers no substantive AI Act obligations in its own right. It is an AI system, so the Regulation applies in principle, but none of the operative duty regimes attach on these facts. It is not a prohibited practice under Article 5(1): correcting spelling and grammar is not a subliminal, manipulative or deceptive technique materially distorting behaviour so as to cause significant harm (Article 5(1)(a)), does not exploit vulnerabilities of age, disability or social or economic situation (Article 5(1)(b)), performs no social scoring leading to detrimental treatment in unrelated contexts or disproportionate to the person's social behaviour (Article 5(1)(c)(i), (ii)), and involves no biometric identification, facial-image scraping, emotion inference or biometric categorisation (Article 5(1)(d), (h)). It is also not high-risk: it is neither a safety component of an Annex I product nor a use listed in Annex III, so the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements do not apply, no risk-management system, no data-governance duties under Article 10, no Article 13 transparency-to-deployer design or instructions for use (identity of the provider, intended purpose, level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, known or foreseeable risk circumstances, human-oversight measures, expected lifetime and maintenance), no Article 14 human-oversight design (understanding capabilities and limitations, awareness of automation bias, correct interpretation of output), no Article 15 accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity duties, no conformity assessment or CE marking, and no Article 49 registration in the Article 71 EU database, Article 49(2) registration is reserved for providers who conclude, under Article 6(3), that an otherwise Annex III system is not high-risk, which is not this case. The Article 50 transparency duties are also not engaged on a pure correction function. Article 50(1) covers systems intended to interact directly with natural persons and requires disclosure of the AI nature of the interaction; an inline correction tool is not a conversational interface, though a chat-style writing assistant added to the same product would need that disclosure unless the AI nature is obvious to a reasonably well-informed user. Article 50(2) machine-readable marking applies to providers of systems generating synthetic text, image, audio or video; localised spelling and grammar corrections to the user's own text are not synthetic content generation, but a generative rewrite, drafting or summarisation feature in the same product would fall within it. Article 50(3) (emotion recognition, biometric categorisation) and Article 50(4) (deepfake labelling) are inapplicable; the Article 50(4) fourth-subparagraph duty to disclose AI-generated or manipulated text applies only to text published to inform the public on matters of public interest, and even then not where publication is authorised by law for detecting, preventing, investigating or prosecuting criminal offences, or where the text has undergone human review or editorial control with a natural or legal person bearing editorial responsibility, the author's own review of their document satisfies that carve-out. Two residual points. First, the Article 4 AI literacy duty applies horizontally to providers and deployers of any AI system, so the vendor and any organisation deploying the word processor must take measures to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy among the staff dealing with it, having regard to their technical knowledge, training and context of use. Second, if the feature is built on a general-purpose AI model, the Chapter V obligations fall on the model provider, not the word-processor vendor: Annex XI technical documentation (Article 53(1)(a)), downstream-provider information per Annex XII (Article 53(1)(b)), a copyright-compliance policy (Article 53(1)(c)) and a publicly available sufficiently detailed training-content summary (Article 53(1)(d)), with Article 53(2) exempting points (a) and (b), but not (c) and (d), for free and open-source models with publicly available parameters, unless the model is designated as systemic-risk under Article 51, in which case the Article 55 duties also apply. The word-processor vendor inherits those provider duties only if it fine-tunes or modifies the model to the extent that it becomes the provider of a new model. Breaches of Chapter V are enforced by the Commission through the AI Office, with fines up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3 % of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher (Article 101(1)).

The difference is one of legal classification and consequent regulatory burden: "high-risk" is a defined statutory category triggered by the classification rules in Article 6, which pulls the system into the full Chapter III requirement set and its registration and conformity machinery, whereas "minimal risk" is not a classification the Regulation operatively defines at all, it is the residual position of any system that is not caught by those rules, and it therefore attracts none of the high-risk product requirements. An AI system is high-risk on either of two routes. Under the Annex I product route (Article 6(1)), both conditions must be met cumulatively: the AI system is intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or is itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I (machinery, toys, recreational craft, lifts, ATEX equipment, radio equipment, pressure equipment, cableways, personal protective equipment, gas appliances, medical devices, in vitro diagnostic medical devices, civil aviation security, two- or three-wheel and quadricycle vehicles, agricultural and forestry vehicles, marine equipment, rail interoperability, motor vehicles, vehicle general safety, and civil aviation); and that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation with a view to its placing on the market or putting into service. Under the Annex III route (Article 6(2)), systems referred to in Annex III are high-risk, the eight areas being biometrics (in so far as permitted under Union or national law), critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and workers' management and access to self-employment, access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits, law enforcement, migration and asylum and border control management, and administration of justice and democratic processes, but only where the system matches one of the lettered use-cases listed under an area, not merely because it operates in that sector. Article 6(3) provides the derogation that marks the boundary with lower-risk systems: an Annex III system is not high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision-making, and it is intended to perform a narrow procedural task (point (a)), to improve the result of a previously completed human activity (point (b)), to detect decision-making patterns or deviations from prior decision-making patterns and is not meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment without proper human review (point (c)), or to perform a preparatory task to an assessment relevant for the Annex III use cases (point (d)). Notwithstanding those conditions, a system performing profiling of natural persons is always high-risk (Article 6(3), point (d), final subparagraph). A provider relying on the derogation must document its assessment before the system is placed on the market or put into service and must still register itself and the system in the EU database (Article 49(2)), so even the derogated system is not treated identically to a genuinely minimal-risk one. The practical consequence of classification is the requirement set. A high-risk system must satisfy the Section 2 requirements of Chapter III, including data governance over training, validation and testing sets, design choices, data collection and origin, preparation operations, assumptions, assessment of availability and suitability, bias examination and mitigation, and identification of data gaps (Article 10(2), points (a) to (h)), and appropriate accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity performing consistently throughout the lifecycle, with accuracy metrics declared in the instructions for use and resilience against data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples or model evasion, confidentiality attacks and model flaws (Article 15(1), (3) and (5)). Compliance may be established through presumptions: conformity with harmonised standards published in the Official Journal (Article 40(1)), training and testing on data reflecting the specific geographical, behavioural, contextual or functional setting of intended use for the purposes of Article 10(4) (Article 42(1)), and certification under a cybersecurity scheme pursuant to Regulation (EU) 2019/881 for the Article 15 cybersecurity requirements, to the extent covered (Article 42(2)). Registration is also required: providers and authorised representatives must register themselves and the Annex III system in the EU database before placing it on the market or putting it into service, except for systems under point 2 of Annex III (Article 49(1)); deployers that are public authorities, Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies, or persons acting on their behalf, must register themselves and the use of the system, again excepting point 2 of Annex III (Article 49(3)); and point 2 systems are registered at national level instead (Article 49(5)). That database is the EU database maintained by the Commission under Article 71(1), which also holds systems registered as non-high-risk under Article 6(3). A minimal-risk system, by contrast, meets neither Article 6(1) nor Article 6(2), and so none of those requirements, presumptions or registration duties attach to it; it may be developed and used without the Chapter III Section 2 obligations, subject only to whatever general duties apply irrespective of risk classification.

On the facts as described, this is aggressive marketing rather than a prohibited practice: it does not satisfy the cumulative conditions of Article 5(1)(a), because the element of significant harm is missing. Article 5(1)(a) prohibits placing on the market, putting into service or use of an AI system that deploys subliminal techniques beyond a person's consciousness or purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques, but only where four conditions hold together, (i) one of those techniques is deployed; (ii) the system has the objective or the effect of materially distorting the behaviour of a person or group; (iii) it does so by appreciably impairing their ability to make an informed decision, thereby causing them to take a decision they would not otherwise have taken; and (iv) that occurs in a manner that causes or is reasonably likely to cause that person, another person or a group significant harm. The operator's facts plausibly meet the first three limbs: a haptic pulse whose persuasive function and AI-selected timing operate outside the user's awareness can be characterised either as a subliminal technique beyond consciousness (the buzz is felt, but its manipulative role at the hesitation moment is not perceived) or as a purposefully manipulative technique, and its whole design objective is to reverse a decision the user was about to take. The prohibition nonetheless fails at the fourth limb: a recovered in-app purchase of ordinary value, freely priced and reversible under consumer law, is not significant harm to health, safety, financial interests or fundamental rights. Article 5(1)(a) is not a general ban on manipulative marketing; it is a ban on manipulation that reaches a significant-harm threshold. Two qualifications constrain that conclusion. First, the assessment changes if the same technique is aimed at, or predictably lands on, persons whose vulnerabilities arise from age, disability or a specific social or economic situation, minors, or users the system can identify as financially distressed, since Article 5(1)(b) prohibits exploitation of exactly those vulnerabilities where behaviour is materially distorted in a manner causing or reasonably likely to cause significant harm; note that limb (b) requires no subliminal or deceptive quality at all, only exploitation plus the same harm threshold. Second, harm is measured on a reasonable-likelihood basis and cumulatively, so a system that repeatedly drives high-frequency or high-value spending, or spending of a compulsive character, can cross into significant financial harm and thereby into the prohibition even though any single buzz would not. Finally, a negative verdict under Article 5 is not a clearance under Union law generally: Article 5(8) provides that the Article does not affect prohibitions applying where an AI practice infringes other Union law, so the practice remains assessable as an aggressive or misleading commercial practice under consumer protection law and against the data protection rules governing the hesitation-signal profiling that drives the timing.

Yes, Article 5(1)(c) applies fully to a private insurer. The prohibition is drafted by conduct, not by actor: it bans the placing on the market, putting into service or use of an AI system for the evaluation or classification of natural persons or groups over a certain period of time on the basis of their social behaviour or known, inferred or predicted personal or personality characteristics, where the resulting social score leads to either or both of the two listed effects. Nothing in Article 5(1)(c) confines it to public authorities, and Recital 31 confirms that social scoring "by public or private actors" is the target; Article 2's scope reaches any provider or deployer placing such a system on the Union market or using it in the Union. Both limbs must be checked, and only one need be met. Limb (i) catches detrimental or unfavourable treatment of certain natural persons or groups in social contexts that are unrelated to the contexts in which the data was originally generated or collected. Limb (ii) catches detrimental or unfavourable treatment that is unjustified or disproportionate to the social behaviour or its gravity. On the facts described, limb (i) is squarely engaged: social-media activity is generated in a social/expressive context wholly unrelated to insurance contracting, and the score restricts access to products, a detrimental effect. Limb (ii) is independently likely engaged, because a general "trustworthiness" rating derived from unrelated online behaviour is disproportionate to the gravity of that behaviour as a basis for denying products. The decisive qualifier is generality. Per Recital 31's final sentence, the prohibition does not affect lawful evaluation practices of natural persons carried out for a specific purpose in accordance with Union and national law. An insurer that assesses a defined, legally grounded risk factor using data relevant to that specific purpose stays outside Article 5(1)(c); what is prohibited is the aggregate, cross-context score of general social worth that then travels into unrelated decisions. The aggregation of social-media activity into a general trustworthiness rating is the paradigm of the prohibited conduct rather than the carve-out. If the insurer were to reconfigure the system into a lawful, purpose-specific evaluation, it would not thereby escape the Regulation: AI systems used for risk assessment and pricing in relation to natural persons in life and health insurance are high-risk under Annex III, point 5(c), and systems evaluating creditworthiness or establishing a credit score are high-risk under Annex III, point 5(b) (save systems used for detecting financial fraud), with classification confirmed through Article 6(2) and the Article 6(3) derogation unavailable wherever the system performs profiling of natural persons. Article 5(8) also preserves prohibitions arising where the practice infringes other Union law, notably data-protection law governing the repurposing of social-media data.

Prohibited. An AI system placed on the market, put into service for that specific purpose, or used to make risk assessments of natural persons in order to assess or predict the risk of a natural person committing a criminal offence, based solely on the profiling of that person or on assessing their personality traits and characteristics, falls squarely within the prohibited practice in Article 5(1), point (d), and is therefore banned outright rather than merely regulated as high-risk. The sole carve-out in that same point does not help here: the prohibition does not apply to AI systems used to support the human assessment of the involvement of a person in a criminal activity which is already based on objective and verifiable facts directly linked to a criminal activity, and on the facts given there are no objective facts tied to a specific offence, so the profiling-only basis brings the system within the ban. Article 5(8) further confirms that this prohibition operates without prejudice to prohibitions arising under other Union law. The Annex III law-enforcement route is not available as an alternative characterisation on these facts. Annex III, point 6(d) classifies as high-risk only systems used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities (or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies supporting them) for assessing the risk of a natural person offending or re-offending not solely on the basis of profiling as referred to in Article 3(4) of Directive (EU) 2016/680, or to assess personality traits and characteristics or past criminal behaviour; the "not solely" qualifier means a purely profiling-based predictor of first offending is excluded from that high-risk use-case and captured by the Article 5(1)(d) ban instead. Nor do the neighbouring law-enforcement use-cases apply: point 6(a) covers assessing the risk of becoming a victim of criminal offences, point 6(b) polygraphs and similar tools, point 6(c) evaluating the reliability of evidence in investigation or prosecution, and point 6(e) profiling within Article 3(4) of Directive (EU) 2016/680 in the course of detection, investigation or prosecution of criminal offences, none of which describes the system as posed. A system would only move into the high-risk regime if it were redesigned so that the assessment rests on more than profiling or personality traits alone, and even then Annex III, point 6 applies only in so far as such use is permitted under relevant Union or national law.

Yes, this use is permitted, but only as a narrow derogation from a prohibited practice, and only if every condition attaching to it is met; absent those conditions the same deployment is a prohibited practice under Article 5(1)(h). Real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes is prohibited under Article 5(1), first subparagraph, point (h), unless and in so far as it is strictly necessary for one of three exhaustive objectives: (i) the targeted search for specific victims of abduction, trafficking in human beings or sexual exploitation, and the search for missing persons; (ii) the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to the life or physical safety of natural persons, or of a genuine and present or genuine and foreseeable threat of a terrorist attack; and (iii) the localisation or identification of a person suspected of having committed a criminal offence, for the purpose of a criminal investigation, prosecution or execution of a criminal penalty, for offences listed in Annex II and punishable in the Member State concerned by a custodial sentence or detention order for a maximum period of at least four years (Article 5(1)(h)(i), (iii)). A square-based search for a suspect in an imminent terrorist attack falls within limb (ii), and, where the suspect is sought in connection with a terrorism offence meeting the four-year threshold, also within limb (iii), terrorism being listed in Annex II. Point (h) is without prejudice to Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 for processing of biometric data for non-law-enforcement purposes. The deployment must then satisfy Article 5(2): it may be used only to confirm the identity of the specifically targeted individual, and must take into account (a) the nature of the situation, in particular the seriousness, probability and scale of the harm that would be caused if the system were not used, and (b) the consequences of use for the rights and freedoms of all persons concerned, in particular the seriousness, probability and scale of those consequences. It must comply with necessary and proportionate safeguards and conditions under the national law authorising the use, in particular as regards temporal, geographic and personal limitations, so a square-wide deployment must be bounded in time, area and target set. Use is authorised only if the law-enforcement authority has completed a fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27 and has registered the system in the EU database under Article 49; in duly justified cases of urgency, use may be commenced without the registration provided registration is completed without undue delay. For law-enforcement systems the Article 49 registration is made in the secure non-public section of the EU database, accessible only to the Commission and the authorities referred to in Article 74(8) (Article 49(4)). Each use additionally requires prior authorisation granted by a judicial authority or an independent administrative authority of the Member State whose decision is binding, issued on reasoned request and only where the authority is satisfied the use is necessary for and proportionate to the objective identified (Article 5(3)). In a duly justified situation of urgency, use may begin without prior authorisation provided authorisation is requested without undue delay and at the latest within 24 hours; if that authorisation is refused, use must stop with immediate effect and all data, results and outputs must be immediately discarded and deleted (Article 5(3)). No adverse legal decision may be taken solely on the basis of the system's output. Each use must be notified to the relevant market surveillance authority and the national data protection authority, excluding disclosure of sensitive operational data (Article 5(4)). Critically, the derogation is not self-executing: it operates only where the Member State has decided to provide, in national law, for the possibility to authorise such use fully or partially, within the limits and conditions of Article 5(1)(h), (2) and (3), and has laid down the detailed national rules for requesting, issuing, exercising and supervising the authorisations; Member States may also maintain or introduce more restrictive laws, up to a complete national ban (Article 5(5)). If the relevant Member State has not enacted such an authorising framework, the police deployment remains prohibited notwithstanding the terrorist-threat objective. Finally, lawfulness under Article 5 does not exhaust the regime. A remote biometric identification system is a high-risk AI system under Annex III, point 1(a), read with Article 6(2), so the provider must meet the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements and the Article 16 obligations (quality management, technical documentation, logging, conformity assessment under Article 43, EU declaration of conformity, CE marking, registration under Article 49), and the police force as deployer must use the system in accordance with the instructions for use (Article 26(1)), assign human oversight to competent, trained and adequately resourced natural persons (Article 26(2)), monitor operation and inform the provider of serious incidents (Article 26(5)), retain the automatically generated logs under its control for at least six months unless Union or national law provides otherwise (Article 26(6)), and, as a public authority, comply with the Article 49 registration duties and refrain from using an unregistered system (Article 26(8)).

The vendor's marketing label does not control the classification: a webcam tool that infers a student's confusion from facial data is an emotion recognition system within the meaning of Article 3(39), an AI system for identifying or inferring emotions or intentions of natural persons on the basis of their biometric data, facial images being biometric data under Article 3(34), and where it is used in education institutions its use, placing on the market and putting into service for that purpose are prohibited under Article 5(1)(f), the only carve-out being systems intended to be put in place or on the market for medical or safety reasons. Detecting confusion so a teacher can intervene pedagogically is neither a medical nor a safety purpose, so the carve-out is unavailable.
