Recital 18 confirms the reach of the definition: confusion is an inferred affective/cognitive state rather than a mere physical state such as pain or fatigue, and the exclusion for "mere detection of readily apparent expressions, gestures or movements" falls away precisely where those expressions are used to infer an emotion or intention, which is what this tool does. Recital 44 explains the rationale, the scientific fragility of emotion inference combined with the power imbalance in education contexts. That the system is also "adaptive" is legally neutral: adaptiveness after deployment is part of the Article 3(1) definition of an AI system, not a reason to exit the Act. The one genuinely unresolved condition is whether the online-learning platform operates in "the area of education institutions" for Article 5(1)(f) purposes. Where it is supplied to, or operates within, schools, universities or vocational training institutions, including remote delivery of their teaching, the prohibition applies and no compliance package can cure it; the deployer school and the vendor are both exposed, and any natural or legal person may complain to the market surveillance authority under Article 85. If, exceptionally, the deployment falls outside that area (for instance a purely private consumer offering unconnected to an educational or vocational training institution), the system is not thereby unregulated: it is high-risk under Article 6(2) via Annex III.1, which lists emotion recognition systems other than those prohibited, and it may be independently caught by Annex III.3(b), covering AI systems intended to evaluate learning outcomes including where those outcomes are used to steer the learning process in educational and vocational training institutions at all levels. The Article 6(3) derogation will not rescue it: continuous per-student inference of affective states is not a narrow procedural task, an improvement of a previously completed human activity, a pattern-detection exercise that neither replaces nor influences a completed human assessment, nor a preparatory task, and in any event the derogation is unavailable where the system performs profiling of natural persons within Article 3(52), which persistent evaluation of individual learners' states will ordinarily amount to; the provider must document that self-assessment before placing the system on the market. On that high-risk footing the vendor, as provider, carries the Article 16 package: compliance with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements, identification on the system, a quality management system under Article 17, technical documentation under Articles 11 and 18, retention of automatically generated logs under Article 19 for a period appropriate to the intended purpose and at least six months, conformity assessment under Article 43, the EU declaration of conformity under Article 47, CE marking under Article 48, registration in the EU database under Article 49, corrective action under Article 20, and demonstration of compliance to authorities on request under Article 21. It must design the system for effective human oversight under Article 14(1) and hand it over so that the teachers assigned oversight can understand its capacities and limitations and monitor its operation (Article 14(4)(a)), remain aware of automation bias (Article 14(4)(b)), correctly interpret its output (Article 14(4)(c)), decide not to use it or to disregard, override or reverse its output (Article 14(4)(d)), and intervene or stop it (Article 14(4)(e)). The platform operator or school, as deployer, must use it in accordance with the instructions for use with appropriate technical and organisational measures (Article 26(1)) and monitor operation and inform the provider of serious incidents (Article 26(5)). Independently of risk class, Article 50(3) obliges the deployer of an emotion recognition system to inform the natural persons exposed to it of the system's operation and to process the personal data in accordance with Regulations (EU) 2016/679 and (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680; the sole exception is for biometric categorisation and emotion recognition permitted by law to detect, prevent or investigate criminal offences subject to safeguards, which plainly does not cover classroom use. That information must be given clearly and distinguishably at the latest at the time of first exposure and must meet the applicable accessibility requirements (Article 50(5)), and these duties are without prejudice to the Chapter III requirements (Article 50(6)). Students subject to a decision taken on the basis of the system's output that produces legal effects or similarly significant adverse effects on their health, safety or fundamental rights may require from the deployer a clear and meaningful explanation of the system's role and the main elements of the decision under Article 86, and Article 2(7) preserves the full application of Union data protection law, including the Article 9 GDPR regime for biometric data.

Minimal-risk. An AI feature that tags and clusters a user's own private photos by content attracts no obligation under the Act beyond the general rules applicable to all AI systems. It is not high-risk on either route. There is no Annex I route: the tagging function is neither a product nor a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I requiring third-party conformity assessment (Article 6(1)). There is no Annex III route either: content tagging in a consumer gallery matches none of the lettered use-cases under the eight areas of biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and workers' management, essential private and public services, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control, and administration of justice and democratic processes (Article 6(2)). Because no Annex III use-case is engaged, the Article 6(3) derogation and its profiling proviso never come into play. None of the Article 50 limbs bites. The system is not intended to interact directly with natural persons in the sense of Article 50(1); it does not generate synthetic audio, image, video or text, so the machine-readable marking duty in Article 50(2) does not arise; it is not an emotion-recognition or biometric-categorisation system triggering the deployer's duty to inform exposed persons under Article 50(3); and it produces no deep fake or public-interest text requiring disclosure under Article 50(4). The classification would change only if the face-grouping function were built to infer sensitive or protected attributes, which would engage the Article 5(1)(g) prohibition on biometric categorisation, or were offered as a remote biometric identification system under Annex III(1).

Yes, but the obligations are narrow: an AI translation feature in an email client is neither a prohibited practice nor a high-risk system, so the only duties in play are the Article 50 transparency rules on the provider, plus scope and residual-law provisions. The Act applies in the first place under Article 2(1)(a), (c): the provider placing the email client with its embedded AI translation on the Union market is covered irrespective of establishment, as are third-country providers and deployers whose output is used in the Union, and deployers established in the Union. A natural person using the feature to read their own private mail is outside the Act's deployer obligations under Article 2(10) (purely personal, non-professional activity), whereas an employer or business rolling the client out to staff is a deployer. Article 2(7) preserves the full application of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 and Directive 2002/58/EC to the personal data and communications content processed, and Article 50(6) confirms Article 50 is without prejudice to other Union or national transparency obligations. The system is not high-risk. The Annex I route in Article 6(1) is not engaged: message translation is not a safety component of, nor itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I subject to third-party conformity assessment. The Annex III route in Article 6(2) is not engaged either, because translating incoming correspondence is not a listed use case under any of the eight Annex III areas, biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, essential private and public services, law enforcement, migration/asylum/border control, or administration of justice and democratic processes. Because no Annex III use case is met, the Article 6(3) derogation is not reached at all, and no Article 6(4) documented self-assessment is required. It follows that none of Articles 13, 16, 21, 26, 43, 44, 49 or 72 apply: no instructions for use under Article 13(2), (3), no quality-management system, technical documentation, CE marking, EU database registration, conformity assessment, deployer human-oversight or six-month log retention, and no post-market monitoring system. Nor does any Article 5 prohibition apply, translation involves no subliminal or manipulative technique, no exploitation of vulnerabilities, no social scoring, no criminal-risk profiling, no facial-image scraping, no workplace or educational emotion inference, no sensitive-attribute biometric categorisation, and no real-time remote biometric identification. What remains is Article 50. Article 50(2) is the live duty: a provider of an AI system generating synthetic text must ensure outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated, subject to that paragraph's own exception for systems performing an assistive function for standard editing or not substantially altering the input data or the semantics thereof. Faithful translation preserves the sender's semantics, which points toward the exception, but the point turns on whether the particular implementation substantially alters the input rather than merely rendering it in another language; that is the one condition the provider must resolve and document for itself. Where Article 50 applies, Article 50(5) requires the information to be given clearly and distinguishably at the latest at the time of first interaction or exposure, in accordance with applicable accessibility requirements. Article 50(3) and 50(4) do not bite. There is no emotion recognition or biometric categorisation, so no deployer duty to inform exposed persons; and the deepfake disclosure duty covers image, audio or video content, not translated text. The fourth subparagraph of Article 50(4), artificially generated or manipulated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest, does not cover private incoming correspondence displayed to its recipient, so neither that duty nor its exemptions (authorised criminal-law use; human review or editorial control with a natural or legal person bearing editorial responsibility) are in issue. Finally, if the translation is built on a third party's general-purpose AI model, the Chapter V obligations and the Commission's Article 101 fining powers (up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3 % of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, applicable from 2 August 2026) rest with that model's provider, not the email client vendor; under Article 25 the vendor would itself become a provider only by putting its own name or trademark on the system, making a substantial modification, or changing the intended purpose in a way that makes it high-risk.

No transparency obligation falls on the marketing team as deployer; the only duty triggered here is the provider's marking obligation under Article 50(2). The deployer duties in Article 50(4) do not bite on these facts. The first limb covers deployers of an AI system that generates or manipulates image, audio or video content constituting a deep fake, that is, AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video resembling existing persons, objects, places, entities or events and falsely appearing authentic (Article 3(60)); promotional text is outside that limb both because it is text and because it is not a deep fake. The second limb covers text "published with the purpose of informing the public on matters of public interest"; promotional copy is commercial communication intended to market goods or services, not to inform the public on a matter of public interest, so the duty is not engaged. Even if the copy were treated as public-interest text, that limb is disapplied where the AI-generated content has undergone a process of human review or editorial control and a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility for its publication, which is the ordinary position for marketing copy drafted by AI and then approved and published by the team; the other carve-out, use authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, is irrelevant here. Note that the human-review carve-out is available only for the text limb, not for deep fakes, and that where deep-fake content forms part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work the disclosure is merely limited to an appropriate manner that does not hamper display or enjoyment of the work. What is triggered is the provider-side duty in Article 50(2): the provider of the generative AI system, including a general-purpose AI system, generating synthetic text must ensure the outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated, with technical solutions that are effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as technically feasible, taking into account the specificities and limitations of content types, implementation costs and the generally acknowledged state of the art. That obligation does not apply to the extent the system performs an assistive function for standard editing or does not substantially alter the input data provided by the deployer or the semantics thereof, or where authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences; a system that drafts the copy from a brief goes well beyond assistive standard editing, so the exemption would not cover it. Separately, if the same system is intended to interact directly with natural persons, its provider must design it so that those persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system (Article 50(1)), a provider obligation owed to the marketing staff using it, not a labelling duty owed by the team to the reading public.

Yes, for the duty in Article 50(1) that announcement is sufficient, provided it meets the delivery conditions in Article 50(5). Article 50(1) places the obligation on the provider: AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons must be designed and developed so that the persons concerned are informed that they are interacting with an AI system. A spoken "I am a virtual assistant" delivered by the speaker itself is exactly that design-level disclosure. Article 50(1) itself carries two limits: the duty does not apply where this is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect natural person taking into account the circumstances and context of use, and it does not apply to AI systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences (subject to safeguards for third-party rights). Compliance is conditional on Article 50(5): the information must be provided in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of the first interaction or exposure, and must conform with applicable accessibility requirements. Announcing it before every response satisfies the timing element; an inaudible, hurried or non-accessible rendering would not. The duty is discharged only as to Article 50(1). Article 50(2) still requires the provider to mark synthetic audio output in a machine-readable, detectable format where the assistant generates synthetic content; Article 50(3) separately obliges the deployer to inform exposed persons if emotion recognition or biometric categorisation is used; and Article 50(6) preserves Chapter III requirements and other Union or national transparency obligations.

Yes, the system is high-risk. An AI system used to score and rank applicants for admission falls squarely within Annex III, point 3(a): AI systems intended to be used to determine access or admission, or to assign natural persons to educational and vocational training institutions at all levels. By Article 6(2), an AI system referred to in Annex III is high-risk, and that is the operative route here; the Annex I product route under Article 6(1), safety component of, or itself a product covered by, Union harmonisation legislation and subject to third-party conformity assessment, is not engaged. The vendor's "just a recommendation tool" marketing does not change the classification. Classification turns on the system's intended purpose as listed in Annex III, not on the label attached to its output. The only escape is the derogation in Article 6(3), which applies where the system does not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision-making, and only where one of four conditions is met: (a) the system performs a narrow procedural task; (b) it improves the result of a previously completed human activity; (c) it detects decision-making patterns or deviations from prior patterns and is not meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment without proper human review; or (d) it performs a preparatory task to an assessment relevant to an Annex III use case. Scoring and ranking candidates is not a narrow procedural task, does not merely polish a completed human decision, and is not a mere preparatory step, the ranking is the substance of the selection and materially influences the admission outcome. Decisively, the second subparagraph of Article 6(3) provides that, notwithstanding those conditions, an Annex III system shall always be considered high-risk where it performs profiling of natural persons; an applicant-scoring system evaluating individuals on their personal characteristics does exactly that. If the provider nonetheless maintains the system is not high-risk, Article 6(4) obliges it to document that assessment before placing the system on the market or putting it into service, to register under Article 49(2), and to produce the documentation to national competent authorities on request, a self-assessment that binds the provider rather than immunising the system. The university is the deployer and therefore carries the Article 26 duties: technical and organisational measures to use the system in accordance with the instructions for use (Article 26(1)); assignment of human oversight to natural persons with the necessary competence, training, authority and support (Article 26(2)), without prejudice to other Union or national law duties and to its freedom to organise its own resources (Article 26(3)); ensuring input data is relevant and sufficiently representative in view of the intended purpose, to the extent it controls that data (Article 26(4)); monitoring operation on the basis of the instructions and informing the provider under Article 72, plus, where use may result in a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), informing the provider or distributor and the market surveillance authority without undue delay and suspending use, and immediately reporting any serious incident first to the provider then to the importer or distributor and the market surveillance authorities, with Article 73 applying mutatis mutandis if the provider cannot be reached (Article 26(5)); keeping automatically generated logs under its control for a period appropriate to the intended purpose and at least six months unless Union or national law, in particular data protection law, provides otherwise (Article 26(6)); where the university is a public authority, complying with the Article 49 registration obligations and refusing to use a system not registered in the EU database referred to in Article 71, informing the provider or distributor (Article 26(8)); using the Article 13 information to carry out any data protection impact assessment required under Article 35 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (Article 26(9)); informing applicants that they are subject to the use of the high-risk AI system, since it makes or assists in making decisions relating to natural persons (Article 26(11)); and cooperating with the competent authorities in any action they take regarding the system (Article 26(12)).

Yes, if the system in substance evaluates the creditworthiness of natural persons, it is high-risk, and the "marketing prioritisation" label does not change that. Classification under Article 6(2) turns on the use-case listed in Annex III, and Annex III, point 5(b) covers AI systems intended to be used to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons or establish their credit score, with the single carve-out for systems used for the purpose of detecting financial fraud. A tool that ranks loan applicants by their likely credit outcome so staff know whom to pursue is performing that evaluative function regardless of the internal name given to it; the fraud-detection exception is unavailable because the purpose here is applicant selection, not fraud detection. If, by contrast, the ranking genuinely uses only contact-propensity or channel-preference signals and no assessment of repayment capacity, risk or score, Annex III point 5(b) is not engaged, but that must be demonstrable from the model's inputs, outputs and intended purpose, not asserted by naming. The Article 6(3) derogation does not rescue this system. That derogation requires both no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights and one of four conditions, the system performs a narrow procedural task; it improves the result of a previously completed human activity; it detects decision-making patterns or deviations from prior decision-making patterns without replacing or influencing the previously completed human assessment without proper human review; or it performs a preparatory task to an assessment relevant to the Annex III use-case. Pre-screening might superficially look like a preparatory task, but the derogation is expressly disapplied where the AI system performs profiling of natural persons, in which case it is always high-risk. Scoring individual applicants on personal and financial characteristics is such profiling, so the exclusion applies. Under Article 6(4), a provider who nonetheless considers the system not high-risk must document that assessment before placing it on the market or putting it into service, is subject to the Article 49(2) registration obligation, and must supply the documentation to national competent authorities on request. Two consequences follow for the bank. If it merely uses a third-party tool, it is a deployer; but if it puts its name or trademark on the system, makes a substantial modification, or modifies the intended purpose so that the system becomes high-risk, it is treated as the provider and assumes the Article 16 provider obligations (Article 25(1)(a), (c)). Independently of classification, Article 4(1) requires the bank, as provider or deployer, to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy among staff and others operating the system on its behalf.

Full high-risk treatment, with the Article 50 disclosure applying on top rather than instead. The symptom-triage function is not a general enquiry service: an AI system used for patient triage that establishes priority in the delivery of emergency care falls within the Annex III, point 5 area (access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits), and is therefore high-risk under Article 6(2). The benign "general questions" component does not dilute that. Classification attaches to the system's intended purpose within the meaning of Article 3(12), the use for which the provider intends it, as specified in the instructions for use, promotional materials and technical documentation, and a single system placed on the market with a stated triage purpose is high-risk as a whole; only genuinely separating the two into distinct systems, with the triage capability absent from the enquiry product, would leave the enquiry chatbot in limited-risk territory. The Article 6(3) derogation is not available. Urgency triage that routes care is none of the four alternatives: it is not a narrow procedural task, it does not merely improve the result of a previously completed human activity, it does not merely detect decision-making patterns or deviations from prior decision-making patterns without replacing or influencing a human assessment (it directly shapes the clinical routing decision), and it is not preparatory to a human assessment in the sense contemplated. Each limb also requires the absence of significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, which mis-triage of symptoms plainly does not satisfy; and if the system profiles natural persons it is high-risk in every case. A provider who nonetheless concluded otherwise would have to document that assessment before placing the system on the market under Article 6(4) and register under Article 49(2), and produce the documentation to national competent authorities on request. The Annex I route must be checked separately and before any derogation reasoning. If the triage functionality is intended by the manufacturer for a medical purpose, the software is a medical device under the sectoral regime, and where that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment, Article 6(1) makes it high-risk independently of Annex III. In that case Article 43(3) integrates the AI Act assessment into the notified-body procedure under the Medical Device Regulation, one procedure, one CE marking. On the Annex III route alone, Article 43(2) applies (the Annex VI internal-control procedure, the Annex VII notified-body procedure being reserved by Article 43(1) to Annex III, point 1 biometric systems). Either way, Article 43(4) requires a fresh conformity assessment on any substantial modification, and Article 49(1) requires registration in the EU database before placing on the market or putting into service, Annex III point 5 not being within the point 2 carve-out. The hospital, as deployer, is a body providing a public service and must carry out the fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27 before first use, covering the processes in which the system will be used in line with its intended purpose, the period and frequency of use, the categories of natural persons affected, the specific risks of harm to them, the human-oversight measures, and the governance and complaints arrangements. The Article 27(1) exclusion covers only Annex III, point 2 systems and does not help here. Article 50 is additive, not alternative: Article 50(6) states expressly that paragraphs 1 to 4 do not affect the requirements and obligations in Chapter III. The provider must still ensure under Article 50(1) that patients are informed they are interacting with an AI system, with that information given clearly and distinguishably at the latest at the time of the first interaction, unless it is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person from the circumstances and context of use. If the chatbot generates synthetic text, Article 50(2) requires outputs to be marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated, using solutions that are effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as technically feasible; that marking duty does not apply to the extent the system performs an assistive function for standard editing or does not substantially alter the input data or its semantics, or where authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences. Article 50(3) and 50(4) are not engaged unless the hospital operates emotion recognition or biometric categorisation, or generates deepfake image, audio or video content.

Because the operator places the system on the EU market under the operator's own name or trademark, the operator is not treated as a mere importer: Article 25(1)(a) deems any distributor, importer, deployer or other third party to be the provider of that high-risk AI system, subject to the full set of provider obligations under Article 16, without prejudice to contractual arrangements allocating those obligations otherwise. The same conversion is triggered by a substantial modification that leaves the system high-risk (Article 25(1)(b)) or by a modification of intended purpose that makes a non-high-risk system high-risk (Article 25(1)(c)); the separate rule in Article 25(3), under which the product manufacturer is the provider where the system is a safety component placed on the market or put into service under the manufacturer's name or trademark, applies only on the Annex I Section A product route, not to Annex III listed uses. Once Article 25(1) bites, the US developer ceases to be the provider of that specific system, but must, under Article 25(2), cooperate closely with you, make available the necessary information and the reasonably expected technical access and other assistance to enable the operator to fulfil the obligations of this Regulation, in particular compliance with the conformity assessment, subject to Article 25(5), which preserves intellectual-property rights, confidential business information and trade secrets. Concretely, the operator must own the substantive Chapter III Section 2 requirements as if you had developed the system: a documented, continuous and iterative risk-management system run across the whole lifecycle, comprising identification and analysis of known and reasonably foreseeable risks in intended use, estimation and evaluation of risks in intended use and under reasonably foreseeable misuse, evaluation of risks arising from post-market monitoring data, and adoption of appropriate and targeted risk-management measures, with testing against preliminarily defined metrics (Article 9); data-governance and management practices for training, validation and testing data sets covering design choices, collection processes and data origin, preparation operations, assumptions, assessment of availability, quantity and suitability, examination for possible biases, measures to detect, prevent and mitigate them, and identification of relevant data gaps (Article 10); technical documentation drawn up before placing on the market and kept up to date with the Annex IV content (Article 11); automatic logging over the system's lifetime enabling traceability for risk identification and substantial modification, post-market monitoring, and monitoring of operation under Article 26(5) (Article 12); sufficient operational transparency and instructions for use giving the operator's identity and contact details, intended purpose, characteristics, capabilities and performance limitations, including tested accuracy metrics, robustness and cybersecurity, foreseeable circumstances affecting them or creating risks to health, safety or fundamental rights, explainability capabilities, performance on specific persons or groups, input-data specifications, log-collection mechanisms and expected lifetime (Article 13); built-in human-oversight measures, including those you identify for the deployer to implement and the ability to disregard, override or reverse the output or not to use the system (Article 14); and appropriate accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, including resistance to data poisoning, model poisoning, evasion and confidentiality attacks (Article 15). Procedurally, the operator must operate a quality management system covering regulatory compliance strategy, design and verification, examination and testing, post-market monitoring and incident reporting (Article 17); carry out the applicable conformity assessment, which for Annex III systems applying harmonised standards or common specifications is the Annex VI internal-control procedure (Article 43); draw up a written, machine-readable, physically or electronically signed and dated EU declaration of conformity per system stating conformity with Section 2, containing the Annex V information, translated for the Member States concerned, kept at the disposal of national competent authorities for 10 years and supplied on request (Article 47); affix the CE marking visibly, legibly and indelibly, or on the packaging or accompanying documentation for digital-only systems, followed by the notified body's identification number where one was involved (Article 48); and register yourself and the system in the EU database before placing it on the market, save for Annex III point 2 systems (Article 49). After placing it on the market the operator must run a post-market monitoring system and plan feeding back into risk management (Article 72) and report serious incidents to the market-surveillance authority of the Member State of occurrence, immediately, and in any event within two days of awareness, for widespread infringement or critical-infrastructure disruption; within 10 days for death; within 15 days for other serious incidents, or immediately upon establishing the causal link (Article 73). The operator must also ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy among the operator's staff and others operating the system on the operator's behalf (Article 4), comply with the Article 50 provider transparency duties where the system interacts directly with natural persons or generates synthetic content, subject to their carve-outs for cases obvious to a reasonably well-informed person and for law-enforcement-authorised detection systems, and without prejudice to Chapter III, and ensure the system involves no practice prohibited by Article 5. The Article 23 importer duties nonetheless remain the compliance floor for the act of bringing the system in and are the checks the operator must satisfy in any event before placing it on the market: verify that the provider carried out the relevant Article 43 conformity assessment, that the technical documentation exists under Article 11 and Annex IV, that the system bears the CE marking and is accompanied by the EU declaration of conformity and instructions for use, and that an authorised representative has been appointed under Article 22(1), this last limb being spent once you yourself, established in the Union, are the provider; refrain from placing the system on the market where you have sufficient reason to consider it non-conforming, falsified or accompanied by falsified documentation until it is brought into conformity, and inform the provider, the authorised representative and market-surveillance authorities where it presents an Article 79(1) risk; indicate the operator's name, registered trade name or trademark and contact address on the system, its packaging or accompanying documentation (Article 23(3)); ensure that storage and transport conditions under the operator's responsibility do not jeopardise Section 2 conformity (Article 23(4)); keep for 10 years a copy of any certificate issued by the notified body, the instructions for use and the EU declaration of conformity (Article 23(5)); supply competent authorities, on reasoned request, with all information and documentation necessary to demonstrate conformity, in a language easily understood by them (Article 23(6)); and cooperate with those authorities on actions to reduce or mitigate risks posed by the system (Article 23(7)).

As a distributor that makes a high-risk AI system available without modifying it, the operator's duties are those of Article 24, and they run from pre-market verification through post-market cooperation. Before making the system available on the market, the operator must verify that it bears the required CE marking, that it is accompanied by a copy of the EU declaration of conformity referred to in Article 47 and by the instructions for use, and that the provider and the importer, as applicable, have complied with their respective obligations under Article 16, points (b) and (c), and Article 23(3) (Article 24(1)). If you consider, or have reason to consider on the basis of information in the operator's possession, that the system is not in conformity with the requirements of Section 2, the operator must not make it available until it has been brought into conformity; and where it presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), the operator must inform the provider or the importer, as applicable (Article 24(2)). While the system is under the operator's responsibility, the operator must ensure that storage or transport conditions, where applicable, do not jeopardise its compliance with the Section 2 requirements (Article 24(3)). For a system you have already made available, if you consider or have reason to consider it non-conforming with Section 2, the operator must take the corrective actions necessary to bring it into conformity, to withdraw it or to recall it, or ensure that the provider, the importer or any relevant operator, as appropriate, takes those actions; and where the system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), the operator must immediately inform the provider or importer and the authorities competent for that system, giving details in particular of the non-compliance and of any corrective actions taken (Article 24(4)). Upon a reasoned request from a relevant competent authority, the operator must provide that authority with all information and documentation regarding the operator's actions under Article 24(1) to (4) necessary to demonstrate the system's conformity with the Section 2 requirements (Article 24(5)), and the operator must cooperate with the relevant competent authorities in any action they take in relation to a high-risk AI system you have made available, in particular to reduce or mitigate the risk it poses (Article 24(6)). These are verification, abstention, custody, corrective-action, information and cooperation duties, as a distributor the operator is not required to build the provider-side compliance apparatus (risk management, data governance, technical documentation, logging, conformity assessment or post-market monitoring), which remains with the provider, provided you continue to act only as a distributor and do not modify the system or place it on the market under the operator's own name or trade mark.

Because cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 floating-point operations, the operator's model is presumed to have high-impact capabilities and is therefore classified as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk (Article 51(1)(a) and 51(2)), which triggers the four additional duties in Article 55(1) on top of the Article 53 obligations: (a) perform model evaluation in accordance with standardised protocols and tools reflecting the state of the art, including conducting and documenting adversarial testing of the model with a view to identifying and mitigating systemic risks; (b) assess and mitigate possible systemic risks at Union level, including their sources, that may stem from the development, the placing on the market, or the use of the model; (c) keep track of, document, and report, without undue delay, to the AI Office and, as appropriate, to national competent authorities, relevant information about serious incidents and possible corrective measures to address them; and (d) ensure an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for both the model itself and the physical infrastructure of the model. These are additive, not substitutive: the Article 53(1) duties continue to apply in full, Annex XI technical documentation kept up to date (Article 53(1)(a)), Annex XII information and documentation for downstream providers integrating the model, sufficient for them to understand its capabilities and limitations and to comply with their own obligations (Article 53(1)(b)(i) and (ii)), a policy to comply with Union copyright law (Article 53(1)(c)), and a publicly available sufficiently detailed summary of the content used for training (Article 53(1)(d)). Critically, the free-and-open-source carve-out that would otherwise disapply Article 53(1)(a) and (b) is expressly unavailable here: Article 53(2) states that the exception does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk, so releasing weights, architecture and usage information publicly does not relieve you of the documentation duties. Two further points on Article 55 itself. Under Article 55(2), you may rely on codes of practice within the meaning of Article 56 to demonstrate compliance with the Article 55(1) obligations until a harmonised standard is published; absent adherence to an approved code or a harmonised standard, the operator must demonstrate alternative adequate means of compliance for assessment by the Commission (mirroring Article 53(4) for the Article 53(1) duties). Note that the Article 56(7) option to limit adherence to the Article 53 obligations is available only to providers not presenting systemic risk, so a code-based route for the operator must cover the full code. Under Article 55(3), any information or documentation obtained pursuant to Article 55, including trade secrets, is to be treated in accordance with the confidentiality obligations of Article 78. Finally, the 10^25 FLOPs figure operates as a rebuttable presumption of high-impact capabilities under Article 51(2), not a conclusive test; classification can equally arise by Commission decision, ex officio or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel, where the model has capabilities or impact equivalent to high-impact capabilities having regard to the Annex XIII criteria (Article 51(1)(b)), and the Commission may amend the thresholds and supplement the benchmarks and indicators by delegated act under Article 51(3).

The provider must appoint, by written mandate, an authorised representative established in the Union, and must do so prior to making the high-risk AI system available on the Union market; this is required by Article 22(1) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. The provider must enable that representative to perform the tasks specified in the mandate (Article 22(2)). Under Article 22(3), the mandate obliges the authorised representative to: verify that the EU declaration of conformity and the technical documentation have been drawn up and that an appropriate conformity assessment procedure has been carried out by the provider (point (a)); keep at the disposal of the competent authorities and national authorities or bodies the contact details of the appointing provider, a copy of the EU declaration of conformity, the technical documentation and, where applicable, the certificate issued by the notified body, for the period specified there (point (b)); provide a competent authority, upon reasoned request, with all information and documentation necessary to demonstrate the system's conformity with the requirements of Section 2, including access to the logs automatically generated by the high-risk AI system referred to in Article 12(1), to the extent such logs are under the provider's control (point (c)); cooperate with competent authorities, upon reasoned request, on any action taken in relation to the high-risk AI system (point (d)); and, where applicable, comply with the registration obligations referred to in Article 49, or, if the registration is carried out by the provider itself, ensure that the information referred to in Annex VIII, Section A, point 3, is correct (point (e)). Registration in the EU database before placing on the market or putting into service may accordingly be effected by the authorised representative (Article 49(1) and, for systems the provider has concluded are not high-risk under Article 6(3), Article 49(2)). The authorised representative must terminate the mandate if it considers or has reason to consider the provider to be acting contrary to its obligations under the Regulation, and must in that case immediately inform the relevant market surveillance authority and, where applicable, the relevant notified body of the termination and its reasons (Article 22(4)). The representative's identity must also appear in the EU declaration of conformity (Annex V).

Article 73 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 governs the reporting of serious incidents involving high-risk AI systems. Under Article 73(1), providers of high-risk AI systems placed on the Union market must report any serious incident, as defined in Article 3, point (49), namely the death of a person or serious harm to a person's health, a serious and irreversible disruption of the management or operation of critical infrastructure, the infringement of obligations under Union law intended to protect fundamental rights, or serious harm to property or the environment, to the market surveillance authorities of the Member States where that incident occurred. The reporting deadlines are tiered. The general rule in Article 73(2) requires the report immediately after the provider has established a causal link between the AI system and the serious incident, or the reasonable likelihood of such a link, and in any event not later than 15 days after the provider or, where applicable, the deployer becomes aware of the incident, the period taking account of the severity of the incident. By way of derogation, Article 73(3) requires an immediate report, and not later than two days after awareness, in the event of a widespread infringement or a serious incident within Article 3, point (49)(b) (critical-infrastructure disruption); Article 73(4) requires, in the event of the death of a person, an immediate report once a causal relationship is established or as soon as it is suspected, and in any event not later than 10 days after awareness. Article 73(5) permits an initial incomplete report where necessary to ensure timely reporting, followed by a complete report. Article 73(6) obliges the provider, following the report, to carry out without delay the necessary investigations, including a risk assessment of the incident and corrective action, to cooperate with the competent authorities and, where relevant, the notified body, and not to alter the AI system in a way that may affect any subsequent evaluation of the causes before informing those authorities. Two scope limitations apply: under Article 73(9), for Annex III high-risk AI systems whose providers are subject to Union legislative instruments laying down equivalent reporting obligations, notification is limited to fundamental-rights incidents under Article 3, point (49)(c); under Article 73(10), for high-risk AI systems that are safety components of devices, or are themselves devices, covered by Regulations (EU) 2017/745 and (EU) 2017/746, notification is likewise limited to Article 3, point (49)(c) incidents and is made to the national competent authority chosen for that purpose by the Member State where the incident occurred. On the authorities' side, Article 73(7) requires the market surveillance authority receiving a fundamental-rights incident notification to inform the national public authorities or bodies referred to in Article 77(1), and mandates Commission guidance by 2 August 2025; Article 73(8) requires that authority to take appropriate measures under Article 19 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 within seven days of receipt; and Article 73(11) requires national competent authorities to notify the Commission immediately of any serious incident, whether or not they have acted on it, in accordance with Article 20 of that Regulation.

Article 57 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 is the provision that establishes AI regulatory sandboxes. Article 57(1) requires each Member State to ensure that its competent authorities establish at least one AI regulatory sandbox at national level, operational by 2 August 2026; that sandbox may be set up jointly with the competent authorities of other Member States, the Commission may provide technical support, advice and tools, and the obligation may alternatively be fulfilled by participating in an existing sandbox in so far as that participation provides an equivalent level of national coverage. Article 57(2) permits additional sandboxes at regional or local level or jointly with other Member States, and Article 57(3) allows the European Data Protection Supervisor to establish a sandbox for Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies, exercising the roles and tasks of national competent authorities. Substantively, Article 57(5) requires such sandboxes to provide a controlled environment that fosters innovation and facilitates the development, training, testing and validation of innovative AI systems for a limited time before their being placed on the market or put into service, pursuant to a specific sandbox plan agreed between the providers or prospective providers and the competent authority, and such sandboxes may include supervised testing in real world conditions. Article 57(6) obliges competent authorities to provide guidance, supervision and support with a view to identifying risks, in particular to fundamental rights, health and safety, testing, mitigation measures and their effectiveness, and Article 57(7) requires guidance on regulatory expectations, written proof of activities successfully carried out upon request, and an exit report usable to demonstrate compliance in conformity assessment or market surveillance. The innovation and SME rationale is set out in Article 57(9), under which the establishment of sandboxes shall aim to contribute to: improving legal certainty to achieve regulatory compliance with the Regulation or, where relevant, other applicable Union and national law; supporting the sharing of best practices through cooperation with the authorities involved; fostering innovation and competitiveness and facilitating the development of an AI ecosystem; contributing to evidence-based regulatory learning; and facilitating and accelerating access to the Union market for AI systems, in particular when provided by SMEs, including start-ups. The supporting safeguards and incentives sit in the same Article: Article 57(4) on sufficient resources, cooperation with other relevant authorities and non-interference with other sandboxes established under Union or national law; Article 57(10) on associating national data protection authorities and other competent authorities where personal data or their supervisory remit is involved; Article 57(11) preserving supervisory and corrective powers, requiring adequate mitigation of significant risks to health, safety and fundamental rights and empowering temporary or permanent suspension of testing or participation with notification to the AI Office; and Article 57(12), under which participants remain liable under applicable Union and national liability law for damage inflicted on third parties, but no administrative fines shall be imposed for infringements of this Regulation provided they observe the specific plan and the terms and conditions of participation and follow in good faith the guidance given by the national competent authority, with the same immunity extending to other Union and national law where the authorities responsible for it were actively involved in supervision and provided compliance guidance. Article 57(8) governs Commission and Board access to exit reports subject to Article 78 confidentiality, Articles 57(13) to 57(15) address cross-border cooperation, coordination within the Board and information to the AI Office, which publishes an up-to-date list of planned and existing sandboxes, Article 57(16) imposes annual and final reporting, and Article 57(17) requires the Commission to develop a single dedicated interface allowing stakeholders to interact with sandboxes and seek non-binding guidance in accordance with Article 62(1), point (c).

Article 99 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 sets out the penalties regime, including the administrative fines for non-compliance. Under Article 99(1), Member States lay down the rules on penalties and other enforcement measures, which may include warnings and non-monetary measures, applicable to infringements by operators, ensuring they are effective, proportionate and dissuasive and taking into account the interests of SMEs, including start-ups, and their economic viability, as well as the Commission's guidelines under Article 96; Article 99(2) requires notification of those rules to the Commission without delay and at the latest by the date of entry into application, and of any subsequent amendment. The fine ceilings are three, each expressed as "whichever is higher" of a fixed amount or a percentage of the offender's total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year where the offender is an undertaking. Up to EUR 35 000 000 or 7 % for non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices referred to in Article 5. Up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3 % for non-compliance with any of the listed provisions related to operators or notified bodies, other than those laid down in Article 5, namely obligations of providers pursuant to Article 16 (point (a)); obligations of authorised representatives pursuant to Article 22 (point (b)); obligations of importers pursuant to Article 23 (point (c)); obligations of distributors pursuant to Article 24 (point (d)); obligations of deployers pursuant to Article 26 (point (e)); requirements and obligations of notified bodies pursuant to Article 31, Article 33(1), (3) and (4) or Article 34 (point (f)); and transparency obligations for providers and deployers pursuant to Article 50 (point (g)). Up to EUR 7 500 000 or 1 % for the supply of incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to notified bodies or national competent authorities in reply to a request. Article 99(6) reverses the rule for SMEs, including start-ups: each fine is up to the percentage or the amount referred to in paragraphs 3, 4 and 5, whichever is lower. Article 99(7) lists the circumstances to be taken into account when deciding whether to impose a fine and on its amount: the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement and its consequences, having regard to the purpose of the AI system and, where appropriate, the number of affected persons and the level of damage; whether fines have already been applied by other market surveillance authorities to the same operator for the same infringement; whether fines have already been applied by other authorities to the same operator for infringements of other Union or national law resulting from the same activity or omission; the size, annual turnover and market share of the operator; any other aggravating or mitigating factor, such as financial benefits gained or losses avoided; the degree of cooperation with the national competent authorities to remedy the infringement and mitigate its adverse effects; the degree of responsibility of the operator, taking into account the technical and organisational measures implemented; the manner in which the infringement became known, in particular whether and to what extent the operator notified it; the intentional or negligent character of the infringement; and any action taken to mitigate the harm suffered by affected persons. Article 99(8) leaves each Member State to determine the extent to which administrative fines may be imposed on public authorities and bodies established in it; Article 99(9) allows fines to be imposed by competent national courts or other bodies depending on the national legal system, provided the rules have equivalent effect; Article 99(10) subjects the exercise of these powers to appropriate procedural safeguards under Union and national law, including effective judicial remedies and due process; and Article 99(11) requires Member States to report annually to the Commission on the fines issued and any related litigation or judicial proceedings.

Article 43 governs the conformity-assessment procedure, Article 47 the EU declaration of conformity, and Article 48 the CE marking, supplemented by Annexes VI and VII (the two assessment procedures) and Annex V (the content of the declaration). On the procedure, Article 43(1) applies to high-risk systems listed in point 1 of Annex III (biometrics): where the provider has applied harmonised standards under Article 40 or, where applicable, common specifications under Article 41, it may choose between conformity assessment based on internal control (Annex VI) or assessment of the quality management system and of the technical documentation with notified-body involvement (Annex VII); the Annex VII route is mandatory where such harmonised standards do not exist and no common specifications are available, where the provider has not applied or has applied only part of the harmonised standard, where common specifications exist but have not been applied, or where a harmonised standard has been published with a restriction and only as to the restricted part. The provider may choose any notified body, save that where the system is to be put into service by law-enforcement, immigration or asylum authorities or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies, the market surveillance authority referred to in Article 74(8) or (9) acts as the notified body. Article 43(2) requires internal control under Annex VI, without notified-body involvement, for systems in points 2 to 8 of Annex III. Article 43(3) covers Annex I, Section A products: the provider follows the sectoral conformity-assessment procedure required by that legislation, with the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements forming part of that single assessment, and points 4.3, 4.4, 4.5 and the fifth paragraph of point 4.6 of Annex VII also applying; notified bodies notified under the sectoral act may control conformity with Section 2 provided their compliance with Article 31(4), (5), (10) and (11) was assessed, and a manufacturer may use a sectoral opt-out from third-party assessment only if it has also applied harmonised standards or common specifications covering all Section 2 requirements. Article 43(4) requires a new conformity assessment upon substantial modification, regardless of further distribution or continued use by the current deployer, while pre-determined changes to continuously learning systems documented under point 2(f) of Annex IV are not substantial modifications. Article 43(5) and (6) empower the Commission to amend Annexes VI and VII, and paragraphs 1 and 2, by delegated act under Article 97. Annex VI comprises verification that the quality management system complies with Article 17, examination of the technical documentation against the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements, and verification that the design and development process and the post-market monitoring under Article 72 are consistent with that documentation. Annex VII comprises assessment and ongoing surveillance of the quality management system (points 3 and 5) and control of the technical documentation (point 4), including notified-body access to training, validation and testing data sets, the power to require further evidence or tests or to test directly, reasoned access to the training and trained models and their parameters as a last resort subject to intellectual-property and trade-secret law, issuance or refusal of a Union technical-documentation assessment certificate, and assessment of changes affecting compliance or intended purpose under point 4.7. Under Article 47(1) the provider must draw up a written, machine-readable, physically or electronically signed EU declaration of conformity for each high-risk AI system, identifying that system, keep it at the disposal of national competent authorities for 10 years after placing on the market or putting into service, and submit a copy on request. Article 47(2) requires it to state that the system meets the Section 2 requirements, to contain the Annex V information, and to be translated into a language easily understood by the competent authorities of the Member States concerned; Article 47(3) requires a single declaration covering all applicable Union harmonisation legislation where that legislation also requires one; Article 47(4) attaches responsibility for Section 2 compliance and a duty to keep the declaration up to date; Article 47(5) empowers the Commission to amend Annex V. Annex V requires the system name and type plus any additional unambiguous reference enabling identification and traceability; the name and address of the provider or, where applicable, the authorised representative; a statement that the declaration is issued under the provider's sole responsibility; a statement of conformity with the Regulation and any other relevant Union law requiring such a declaration; where personal data is processed, a statement of compliance with Regulations (EU) 2016/679 and (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680; references to harmonised standards or other common specifications applied; where applicable, the name and identification number of the notified body, a description of the conformity assessment performed and identification of the certificate issued; and the place and date of issue, the name and function of the signatory, the person for or on behalf of whom it was signed, and a signature. On marking, Article 48(1) subjects the CE marking to the general principles in Article 30 of Regulation (EC) No 765/2008; Article 48(2) requires a digital CE marking for digitally provided systems, only if easily accessible via the interface through which the system is accessed or via an easily accessible machine-readable code or other electronic means; Article 48(3) requires affixing visibly, legibly and indelibly, or, where that is not possible or not warranted by the nature of the system, on the packaging or accompanying documentation; Article 48(4) requires the marking to be followed, where applicable, by the identification number of the notified body responsible for the Article 43 procedures, affixed by that body or under its instructions by the provider or its authorised representative and indicated in any promotional material claiming CE-marking compliance; and Article 48(5) provides that where other Union law also requires CE marking, the marking indicates conformity with that law as well.

The engagement-scoring feature would be a prohibited AI practice, not a risk-tier question: Article 5(1)(f) bans the placing on the market, putting into service for this specific purpose, and use of AI systems to infer emotions of a natural person in the area of the workplace, and the only carve-out is for systems intended to be put in place or into the market for medical or safety reasons. Inferring engagement from employees' facial expressions is exactly an emotion recognition system as understood in the Regulation, identifying or inferring emotions or intentions of natural persons on the basis of their biometric data (Recital 18), and "measuring engagement" is neither a medical nor a safety reason. That the tool is internal, built for the operator's own staff and never sold changes nothing: the prohibition in Article 5(1) bites on use as well as on placing on the market or putting into service, and the operator's employees are the natural persons in the workplace whom that limb is designed to protect. No level of consent, notice or anonymisation cures a prohibited practice, and the transparency route in Article 50(3) for deployers of emotion recognition systems presupposes a system that is lawful in the first place, it does not license one caught by Article 5. Two consequences follow. First, the meeting-notes summarisation function on its own remains outside the high-risk tiers; only the facial-expression layer is the problem, so dropping that layer restores the current position, where the operator's substantive duty is to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy among staff operating the tool under Article 4. Second, if, and only if, the feature were genuinely re-scoped to a medical or safety purpose, it would not become unregulated: emotion recognition sits in the biometrics area of Annex III, so it would be high-risk under Article 6(2), and as the in-house developer putting it into service under the operator's own name you would be the provider (Article 25) and simultaneously the deployer. That would trigger the full Chapter III set, a lifecycle risk management system covering identification and analysis of known and foreseeable risks, estimation of risks under intended purpose and reasonably foreseeable misuse, evaluation of post-market data and targeted mitigation (Article 9(2)); data governance with representative, error-free and complete training, validation and testing sets and bias examination and mitigation (Article 10(2)-(4)); Annex IV technical documentation before putting into service (Article 11(1)); automatic logging (Article 12(1)-(2)); instructions for use stating intended purpose, accuracy metrics, robustness and cybersecurity, foreseeable risks to fundamental rights, explanatory capabilities, performance on specific groups, input-data specifications and output interpretation (Article 13(3)); human oversight (Article 14(2)-(3)); accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity (Article 15); a quality management system (Article 17); conformity assessment (Article 43); an EU declaration of conformity (Article 47); CE marking (Article 48); registration, which for Annex III point 2 systems is at national level (Article 49); post-market monitoring (Article 72); serious-incident reporting (Article 73), plus, as deployer, use per the instructions, oversight by competent and trained persons, monitoring with suspension and notification where a risk or serious incident emerges (Article 26(5)), informing affected workers' representatives before putting the system into service (Article 26(7)), and informing the exposed persons of the operation of the emotion recognition system (Article 50(3)). A fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27(1) would arise only if the operator is a body governed by public law or a private entity providing public services. Practically, the advice is to abandon the facial-expression scoring rather than to engineer around it; a safety-reason relabelling of what is in substance productivity monitoring will not survive scrutiny.

The internal-control procedure under Annex VI applies, with no notified body involved. A CV-sorting system for recruitment falls under the Annex III employment area (recruitment and selection, in particular targeted job advertisements, analysing and filtering applications and evaluating candidates), so it is high-risk on the Annex III route under Article 6(2), not the Annex I product route under Article 6(1); and because it sits in points 2 to 8 of Annex III rather than in point 1 (biometrics), Article 43(2) directs the provider to the conformity assessment based on internal control referred to in Annex VI, which expressly does not provide for the involvement of a notified body. The Annex VII quality-management-system and technical-documentation assessment with a Union technical documentation assessment certificate is therefore not available or required here, and the Article 43(1) choice between Annex VI and which turns on whether harmonised standards under Article 40 or common specifications under Article 41 were applied, is confined to Annex III point 1 systems. Article 43(3) is likewise inapplicable, as it integrates the assessment into the sectoral third-party procedure only for products covered by the Annex I Union harmonisation legislation. Conformity is demonstrated through the three self-executed verification steps of Annex VI: verifying that the established quality management system complies with Article 17 (Annex VI.2); examining the information contained in the technical documentation to assess compliance of the system with the essential requirements of Chapter III, Section 2 (Annex VI.3); and verifying that the design and development process of the system and its post-market monitoring under Article 72 are consistent with that technical documentation (Annex VI.4). The completed documentation and human-oversight measures feed this exercise: the Annex IV technical documentation must be drawn up before placing on the market and kept up to date, in a form allowing national competent authorities to assess compliance (Article 11(1)), and the human-oversight measures under Article 14 must be reflected in the instructions for use (Article 13(3)(d)), alongside any changes to the system and its performance pre-determined by the provider at the moment of the initial conformity assessment (Article 13(3)(c)). Once the Annex VI procedure is passed, and prior to placing on the market, the provider must ensure the system has undergone that procedure (Article 16(1)(f)), draw up the EU declaration of conformity in accordance with Article 47 (Article 16(1)(g)), affix the CE marking to the system or, where that is not possible, to its packaging or accompanying documentation in accordance with Article 48 (Article 16(1)(h)), and comply with the registration obligations of Article 49(1) (Article 16(1)(i)). Conformity must also be demonstrated on demand: upon a reasoned request by a competent authority the provider shall supply all information and documentation necessary to demonstrate conformity with the Section 2 requirements, in an official Union language easily understood by that authority (Article 21(1)), and give access to the automatically generated logs referred to in Article 12(1) to the extent they are under its control (Article 21(2)), with any information so obtained treated under the confidentiality obligations of Article 78 (Article 21(3)), which protect intellectual property rights, confidential business information and trade secrets including source code. A new conformity assessment is required in the event of a substantial modification, regardless of whether the modified system is further distributed or continues to be used by the current deployer; for systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market, changes pre-determined by the provider at the initial conformity assessment and contained in the technical documentation under point 2(f) of Annex IV do not constitute a substantial modification (Article 43(4)). Should a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party put its name or trademark on the system, make a substantial modification, or modify the intended purpose, that actor becomes the provider and assumes the conformity-assessment duty, with the initial provider obliged to cooperate closely and make available the necessary information, reasonably expected technical access and other assistance, subject to intellectual property and trade-secret protection (Article 25(1), (2) and (5)).In that event the fresh assessment again follows the Annex VI internal-control procedure, since the system's classification under the Annex III employment area is unchanged.

Yes. At 3×10²⁵ FLOPs of cumulative training compute the operator's model crosses the threshold in Article 51(2), which presumes high-impact capabilities once cumulative training computation measured in floating-point operations exceeds 10²⁵, and it is therefore classified as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk under Article 51(1)(a). No Commission decision under Article 51(1)(b) on the Annex XIII criteria is needed; that route is an alternative, not a precondition. Note that the presumption attaches to cumulative compute for the model's training, not to the marginal cost of the single run, so the 3×10²⁵ figure must be aggregated with any prior pre-training and subsequent training compute for the same model; the Commission may amend these thresholds by delegated act under Article 51(3). The consequence is additive, not substitutive. You remain subject to the full Article 53(1) baseline: drawing up and keeping up to date the technical documentation of the model, including its training and testing process and evaluation results, containing at a minimum the Annex XI information, for supply on request to the AI Office and national competent authorities (Article 53(1)(a)); drawing up, keeping up to date and making available information and documentation to downstream providers integrating the model, so as to enable them to understand its capabilities and limitations and comply with their own obligations and containing at a minimum the Annex XII elements (Article 53(1)(b)(i), (ii)); putting in place a policy to comply with Union copyright law, in particular identifying and complying with a reservation of rights expressed under Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790, including through state-of-the-art technologies (Article 53(1)(c)); and publishing a sufficiently detailed summary of the content used for training, according to the AI Office template (Article 53(1)(d)). On top of that, Article 55(1) now applies in full: (a) perform model evaluation in accordance with standardised protocols and tools reflecting the state of the art, including conducting and documenting adversarial testing to identify and mitigate systemic risks; (b) assess and mitigate possible systemic risks at Union level, including their sources, stemming from the development, placing on the market or use of the model; (c) keep track of, document and report without undue delay to the AI Office and, as appropriate, to national competent authorities relevant information about serious incidents and possible corrective measures; and (d) ensure an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for both the model and its physical infrastructure. Information and documentation obtained under Article 55, including trade secrets, is handled under the Article 78 confidentiality regime (Article 55(3)). One further change matters if you were relying on a free and open-source release: the Article 53(2) carve-out from the Article 53(1)(a) and (b) documentation duties is expressly unavailable to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk, so licence terms no longer relieve you of the Annex XI and Annex XII obligations. The Article 53(1)(c) copyright policy and (1)(d) training-data summary applied to you in any event. What does not change: crossing 10²⁵ FLOPs does not make the operator's model or any system built on it high-risk. High-risk status is decided separately under Article 6(1) (Annex I product route) or Article 6(2) (an Annex III listed use-case), so Chapter III duties such as Article 14 human oversight and the Article 27 fundamental rights impact assessment arise only if a system based on the model falls within those routes. Article 4 AI literacy continues to apply to the operator in respect of AI systems the operator provides or deploy, and Article 50(1) transparency applies if the operator places on the market a system intended to interact directly with natural persons, unless that is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person, and subject to the carve-out for systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences with appropriate safeguards, which carve-out is itself reversed where the system is available for the public to report a criminal offence.

Yes, you cease to be a mere deployer and are treated as the provider of that high‑risk AI system. Article 25(1) provides that any distributor, importer, deployer or other third party is considered a provider and becomes subject to the provider obligations under Article 16 where (a) they put their name or trademark on a high‑risk AI system already placed on the market or put into service, without prejudice to contractual arrangements stipulating that the obligations are otherwise allocated; (b) they make a substantial modification to a high‑risk AI system already placed on the market or put into service in such a way that it remains high‑risk pursuant to Article 6; or (c) they modify the intended purpose of a non‑high‑risk system so that it becomes high‑risk under Article 6. The operator's facts engage limbs (a) and (b) independently: the rebranding alone suffices, and the substantial modification suffices provided the credit‑scoring system remains high‑risk, which it does, since creditworthiness evaluation of natural persons falls within Annex III, point 5, under the Article 6(2) listed‑use route rather than the Annex I product‑safety route of Article 6(1). The consequence under Article 25(2) is that the initial provider is no longer considered the provider of that specific system, but must cooperate closely, make available the information and the reasonable technical access and other assistance needed for you to fulfil the obligations, unless it has clearly specified that its system is not to be changed into a high‑risk AI system. Article 25(4) likewise contemplates a written agreement with suppliers of tools, services, components or processes specifying the necessary information and technical access. As provider the operator must therefore satisfy the Section 2 requirements in the operator's own name: a risk management system across the lifecycle (Article 9), data and data‑governance quality for training, validation and testing sets (Article 10), technical documentation per Annex IV drawn up before placing on the market (Article 11), automatic logging (Article 12), transparency and instructions for use containing the elements in Article 13(3)(a), (f), including intended purpose, accuracy metrics, foreseeable risks, explanatory capabilities, performance for specific groups, input‑data specifications and output‑interpretation information, human oversight design (Article 14), and accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity (Article 15); plus a quality management system (Article 17). Critically, Article 43(4) requires a new conformity assessment because of the substantial modification, regardless of whether the modified system is further distributed or continues to be used by you as current deployer, via the Annex VI internal‑control procedure for this Annex III system. The operator must then draw up the EU declaration of conformity (Article 47), affix the CE marking (Article 48), register yourself and the system in the EU database before placing it on the market or putting it into service (Article 49(1), the national‑level derogation in Article 49(5) being confined to Annex III point 2), and operate post‑market monitoring (Article 72) and serious‑incident reporting on the tiered deadlines of Article 73. The operator's deployer duties do not disappear where you also continue to use the system: Article 26 obligations (use per the instructions, competent and trained human oversight, input‑data relevance, monitoring) continue, Article 26(11) requires the operator to inform the natural persons subject to the decisions, and the fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27 applies before first use because the system falls under Annex III, point 5(b), covering at minimum the description of the operator's deployment processes and the period and frequency of intended use, together with affected persons, specific risks and human‑oversight and governance measures.

Yes, the classification changes. As a tutoring chatbot that merely discloses its artificial nature, the system is not within any Annex III use-case; once it scores final exams and determines pass/fail, it falls squarely within Annex III point 3(b), AI systems intended to be used to evaluate learning outcomes, including where those outcomes steer the learning process of natural persons in education and vocational training institutions at all levels, and is therefore high-risk under Article 6(2).
