The fact that users are told they are interacting with an AI is a transparency matter and has no bearing on Article 6 classification. If the pass/fail result also governs admission or assignment to an institution, Annex III point 3(a) is engaged as well, and if it determines the appropriate level of education the person will receive or be able to access, point 3(c); invigilation features monitoring for prohibited behaviour during tests would engage point 3(d). The Article 6(3) derogation is not realistically available. It applies only where the system poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights and meets one of four conditions: it performs a narrow procedural task; it improves the result of a previously completed human activity; it detects decision-making patterns or deviations from prior decision-making patterns without replacing or influencing the previously completed human assessment without proper human review; or it performs a preparatory task to an assessment relevant to an Annex III use-case. A system that itself produces the mark and the pass/fail outcome replaces rather than prepares or refines the human assessment. In any event, an Annex III system that performs profiling of natural persons is always high-risk. A provider relying on the derogation must document that assessment before placing on the market or putting into service, is subject to the registration obligation in Article 49(2), and must produce the documentation on request (Article 6(4)). Consequently the full provider regime under Article 16 attaches: compliance with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements, identification markings, a quality management system, technical documentation and logs, conformity assessment under Article 43 before placing on the market, the EU declaration of conformity, CE marking, registration, corrective action, and demonstration of conformity on reasoned request, including Article 10 data governance, Article 15 accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity with accuracy metrics declared in the instructions for use, and retention of documentation for ten years under Article 18. Note also Article 25(1)(c): if a deployer or third party, rather than you, modifies the intended purpose of the already-marketed tutoring system so that it becomes high-risk, that actor becomes the provider and assumes the Article 16 obligations, with the initial provider owing cooperation under Article 25(2). Deploying institutions then owe the Article 26 duties, use per instructions, competent and trained human oversight, monitoring and incident notification, and log retention for at least six months, and, where the deployer is a body governed by public law or a private entity providing public services, a fundamental rights impact assessment before first use under Article 27(1).

Before placing a high-risk AI system on the market, the operator must, under Article 23(1), ensure it is in conformity with the Regulation by verifying four things: (a) that the relevant conformity assessment procedure referred to in Article 43 has been carried out by the provider; (b) that the provider has drawn up the technical documentation in accordance with Article 11 and Annex IV; (c) that the system bears the required CE marking and is accompanied by the EU declaration of conformity referred to in Article 47 and the instructions for use; and (d) that the provider has appointed an authorised representative in accordance with Article 22(1), the written mandate that a third-country provider must give to a representative established in the Union prior to making the system available on the Union market, empowering it inter alia to verify that the Article 47 declaration and Article 11 technical documentation were drawn up and an appropriate conformity assessment was carried out, and to keep that documentation, the certificate where applicable and the provider's contact details at the disposal of competent authorities for 10 years (Article 22(3)(a) and (b)). That verification duty is incomplete without its follow-on steps. Where you have sufficient reason to consider that the system is not in conformity, or is falsified, or accompanied by falsified documentation, the operator must not place it on the market until it has been brought into conformity; and where the system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), the operator must inform the provider, the authorised representative and the market surveillance authorities (Article 23(2)). The operator must also indicate the operator's name, registered trade name or registered trade mark, and the address at which the operator can be contacted on the system and on its packaging or accompanying documentation, where applicable (Article 23(3)), and ensure that, while the system is under the operator's responsibility, storage or transport conditions do not jeopardise its compliance with the Section 2 requirements (Article 23(4)). After placing, the operator must keep for 10 years a copy of the notified body certificate where applicable, the instructions for use and the Article 47 declaration of conformity (Article 23(5)), supply competent authorities on reasoned request with all necessary information and documentation in a language easily understood by them and ensure the technical documentation can be made available to them (Article 23(6)), and cooperate with those authorities in any action they take in relation to the system, in particular to reduce and mitigate the risks it poses (Article 23(7)).

Yes. Before the operator puts the system into use the operator must carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment (FRIA) under Article 27(1). An AI system used by, or on behalf of, a public authority to evaluate the eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits and services, and to grant, reduce, revoke or reclaim such benefits, is high-risk under Annex III, point 5(a), and therefore an Article 6(2) system; as a body governed by public law you fall squarely within the class of deployers Article 27(1) binds. The single exception in Article 27(1), high-risk systems intended to be used in the area listed in point 2 of Annex III (critical infrastructure), does not apply to a housing-benefit eligibility system. The assessment must be performed prior to deployment and must consist of all six elements in Article 27(1): (a) a description of the operator's processes in which the system will be used in line with its intended purpose; (b) a description of the period of time within which, and the frequency with which, the system is intended to be used; (c) the categories of natural persons and groups likely to be affected in the specific context; (d) the specific risks of harm likely to have an impact on those categories, taking into account the information given by the provider under Article 13; (e) a description of the implementation of the human oversight measures, according to the instructions for use; and (f) the measures to be taken should those risks materialise, including internal governance arrangements and complaint mechanisms. Three qualifiers attach to the duty. The obligation applies to the first use of the system, and in similar cases you may rely on a previously conducted fundamental rights impact assessment or on an existing assessment carried out by the provider; if any element listed in Article 27(1) changes or ceases to be up to date during use, the operator must take the necessary steps to update the information (Article 27(2)). Where any of these obligations is already met through a data protection impact assessment under Article 35 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679, the FRIA complements that assessment rather than duplicating it (Article 27(4)). Once performed, the operator must notify the market surveillance authority of the results, submitting the filled-out template that the AI Office is to develop under Article 27(5), save in the Article 46(1) derogation case (Article 27(3)). Separately, and also before first use, Article 26(8) read with Article 49(3) requires you as a public-authority deployer to register yourself in the EU database referred to in Article 71, select the system and register its use; if you find the system has not been registered there, the operator must not use it and must inform the provider or distributor.

Article 10 requires the operator to run the operator's training, validation and testing data sets through a documented data-governance regime and to treat bias examination and mitigation as a design-stage engineering step, not a post-hoc check. The duty bites wherever the operator's high-risk system is developed with techniques involving the training of AI models with data (Article 10(1)); if the operator's system does not involve model training, paragraphs 2 to 5 apply only to the operator's testing data sets (Article 10(6)). Concretely, the governance and management practices must be appropriate to the intended purpose and must cover, in particular: the relevant design choices; the data-collection processes and the origin of the data, and for personal data the original purpose of collection; the relevant data-preparation processing operations such as annotation, labelling, cleaning, updating, enrichment and aggregation; the formulation of assumptions, in particular as to what the data are supposed to measure and represent; an assessment of the availability, quantity and suitability of the data sets needed; examination in view of possible biases likely to affect health and safety of persons, have a negative impact on fundamental rights or lead to discrimination, in particular where data outputs influence inputs for future operations; appropriate measures to detect, prevent and mitigate the biases so identified; and identification of relevant data gaps or shortcomings that prevent compliance, together with how those gaps and shortcomings can be addressed (Article 10(2)(a), (h)). On quality, the data sets must be relevant, sufficiently representative, and to the best extent possible free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose, and must have the appropriate statistical properties, including where applicable as regards the persons or groups of persons in relation to whom the system is intended to be used; those characteristics may be satisfied at the level of an individual data set or at the level of a combination of data sets (Article 10(3)). They must also take into account, to the extent required by the intended purpose, the characteristics or elements particular to the specific geographical, contextual, behavioural or functional setting of intended use (Article 10(4)). Where bias detection and correction requires special categories of personal data, Article 10(5) permits that processing only to the extent strictly necessary and subject to appropriate safeguards, all of which apply cumulatively: the bias detection and correction cannot be effectively fulfilled by processing other data, including synthetic or anonymised data; technical limitations on re-use and state-of-the-art security and privacy-preserving measures, including pseudonymisation, are applied; the data are secured, protected and subject to suitable safeguards including strict controls and documentation of access; the data are not transmitted, transferred or otherwise accessed by other parties; the data are deleted once the bias has been corrected or the retention period ends, whichever comes first; and the records of processing activities under Union data-protection law state why processing those categories was strictly necessary and why the objective could not be achieved by processing other data. This is a narrow derogation resting on the special-category regime of Union data-protection law, so the operator's data-protection documentation and this Article must be aligned rather than treated separately. Operationally, these steps must be embedded as written systems and procedures for data management, acquisition, collection, analysis, labelling, storage, filtration, mining, aggregation, retention and any other pre-market data operation, within the operator's quality management system (Article 17(1)(f)), and the residual bias and representativeness risks identified under Article 10(2)(f) and (g) must feed the identification, evaluation and targeted mitigation steps of the risk-management system (Article 9(2)(a), (d)), since compliance with Article 10 is part of the Section 2 conformity the operator must ensure as provider (Article 16(1)(a) and (c)).

Treat last week's event as a serious incident under a high-risk AI system and act on the deployer's incident chain immediately, an AI system used to evaluate and classify patients for emergency triage falls within Annex III, point 5 (access to and enjoyment of essential public services, including emergency healthcare triage), so it is high-risk under Article 6(2) unless an Article 6(3) derogation was documented, and harm to a patient's health engages the "serious incident" definition in Article 3(49). First, stop and contain. Under Article 26(5) the operator must monitor operation on the basis of the instructions for use and, where you have reason to consider that use in accordance with those instructions may present a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), inform the provider or distributor and the relevant market surveillance authority without undue delay and suspend use of the system. In parallel, verify under Article 26(1) whether the technical and organisational measures actually kept use within the instructions for use, and whether the assigned human overseer could and did override the triage output. Second, preserve the evidence. Article 26(6) requires the operator to keep the logs automatically generated by the system, to the extent they are under the operator's control, for a period appropriate to the intended purpose and in any event at least six months, unless Union or national law, in particular data-protection law, provides otherwise; the provider carries the mirror duty for logs under its control (Article 16(1)(e)). Freeze the relevant case logs now, since they are the input for the provider's incident analysis and for any authority evaluation. Third, the reporting clock. The provider must report the serious incident to the market surveillance authority of the Member State where it occurred, immediately once a causal link (or reasonably likely causal link) between the system and the incident is established and in any event within 15 days of becoming aware; the deadline shortens to 10 days where the incident involves a person's death, and to 2 days for a widespread infringement or a serious and irreversible disruption of critical infrastructure (Article 73(1), (4)). The operator's Article 26(5) notification is what starts that clock, so do not wait for the operator's own root-cause conclusion. Important qualification: if this triage system is itself a medical device, or a safety component of one, covered by Regulation (EU) 2017/745 or (EU) 2017/746 (Annex I, points 11 and 12), Article 73(10) narrows the AI Act track to serious incidents constituting an infringement of Union law protecting fundamental rights, reported to the competent authority designated for that purpose; death or serious deterioration of health routes instead through MDR vigilance reporting by the manufacturer, which the operator's monitoring record feeds. Fourth, the patient. Under Article 86 the affected person subject to a triage decision taken on the basis of the system's output, a decision with significant adverse effects on health, has the right to obtain from you, as deployer, a clear and meaningful explanation of the system's role in the decision-making procedure and of the main elements of the decision, save where Union or national law provides an exception or restriction, and to the extent the right is not already provided under other Union law. Finally, anticipate supervision: the market surveillance authority may evaluate the system under Article 79 and require withdrawal from the market, recall from the distribution chain, or restriction of availability within a period proportionate to the risk, so prepare the operator's logs, oversight records and use documentation for production on request.

Article 86, not Article 13, is the provision that gives the rejected applicant a right to obtain the reasons. Under Article 86, any affected person who is subject to a decision taken by the deployer on the basis of the output of a high-risk AI system listed in with the sole carve-out of Annex III point 2 (critical infrastructure), and where that decision produces legal effects or similarly significantly adversely affects health, safety or fundamental rights, has the right to obtain from the deployer a clear and meaningful explanation of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure and of the main elements of the decision taken. A loan-eligibility system evaluating the creditworthiness of natural persons or establishing their credit score falls squarely within Annex III point 5(b) (the only exclusion there being systems used to detect financial fraud), so the right is engaged and it is owed by you as deployer, not by the provider. The right under Article 86 operates only in so far as it is not already provided for under other Union law, and it complements rather than replaces the safeguards attaching to automated individual decision-making under Article 22 GDPR; it does not extend to information whose disclosure is precluded by the confidentiality protections of Article 78. Article 13 is a distinct and differently addressed duty: it requires the provider to design the high-risk system so that its operation is sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to interpret the output and use it appropriately (Article 13(1)), with an appropriate type and degree of transparency to achieve compliance with the provider's and deployer's obligations (Article 13(2)), delivered through instructions for use containing at least the provider's identity and contact details (Article 13(3)(a)); the characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance, namely intended purpose, the tested level of accuracy with its metrics, robustness and cybersecurity under Article 15 and circumstances affecting it, known or foreseeable circumstances of intended use or reasonably foreseeable misuse leading to risks to health, safety or fundamental rights referred to in Article 9(2), where applicable the technical capabilities to provide information relevant to explaining the output, when appropriate performance regarding specific persons or groups, when appropriate input-data specifications and information on training, validation and testing data sets, and where applicable information enabling deployers to interpret and appropriately use the output (Article 13(3)(b)(i), (vii)); pre-determined changes to the system and its performance (Article 13(3)(c)); the human oversight measures under Article 14 including technical measures facilitating interpretation of outputs (Article 13(3)(d)); the computational and hardware resources, expected lifetime and necessary maintenance and care measures including software updates (Article 13(3)(e)); and where relevant a description of the log-collection, storage and interpretation mechanisms referred to in Article 12 (Article 13(3)(f)). It therefore supplies the material you need in order to satisfy Article 86, but it confers no right on the applicant. Two adjacent duties bear directly on the applicant's position. Because the operator's system makes or assists decisions relating to natural persons, Article 26(11) obliges the operator to inform those persons that they are subject to the use of the high-risk AI system, without prejudice to Article 50. And under Article 85 any natural or legal person may lodge a complaint with the relevant market surveillance authority regarding any infringement, with the authority obliged to inform the complainant of progress and outcome, including possible judicial remedies under Article 86.

Adding an AI reply-suggestion feature does not, by itself, change the classification: the combined spam-filter plus canned-reply product remains outside the high-risk categories and stays a minimal-risk system. Neither classification route in Article 6 is engaged. Under the Annex I route (Article 6(1)), the system is neither a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I nor a safety component of such a product, and there is no product requiring third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation, so the route closes on its own terms. Under the Annex III route (Article 6(2)), generic email triage and reply drafting sold to businesses at large does not correspond to any lettered use case under the eight areas, biometrics; critical infrastructure; education and vocational training; employment, workers' management and access to self-employment; access to and enjoyment of essential private and public services; law enforcement; migration, asylum and border control management; and administration of justice and democratic processes. Because no Annex III use case is met, the Article 6(3) derogation is never reached: it operates only as an exit from Annex III, and with it the Article 6(4) duty to document a not-high-risk self-assessment before placing on the market, and the associated Article 49(2) registration, do not bite either. Consequently none of the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements (including human oversight under Article 14) nor the EU declaration of conformity under Article 47 with the Annex V content apply. Two things would change the outcome, and both turn on intended purpose rather than on the technical addition of a generative feature. First, if the filtering or reply-drafting is intended for a listed use case, the system becomes high-risk under Article 6(2), most realistically Annex III, point 4(a) if it is intended to analyse and filter job applications or otherwise evaluate candidates in recruitment inboxes, Annex III, point 4(b) if it is intended to monitor and evaluate the performance and behaviour of workers or to allocate tasks based on individual behaviour or personal traits, or Annex III, point 5 if it is intended to evaluate eligibility for essential public assistance benefits, creditworthiness, or to triage emergency calls. Note also that an Annex III system that performs profiling of natural persons is always high-risk and cannot use the Article 6(3) derogation. Second, Article 25(1) reallocates provider status: a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party becomes the provider, subject to the Article 16 obligations, where it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk system already on the market (point (a)), makes a substantial modification to a high-risk system such that it remains high-risk under Article 6 (point (b)), or modifies the intended purpose of a system not classified as high-risk, including a general-purpose AI system, so that it becomes high-risk under Article 6 (point (c)). If one of the operator's business customers repurposes the filter for, say, applicant screening, that customer assumes provider obligations, and under Article 25(2) you as initial provider must make available the necessary information and give the reasonably expected technical access and other assistance to enable its conformity assessment. If the reply-suggestion feature is built on a third-party general-purpose AI model that you fine-tune, you do not thereby become the provider of that model unless the Article 51 thresholds and the value-chain rules in Article 25 are triggered; below that, the upstream model provider retains the Article 53 obligations and you remain an integrator or deployer. One narrow point remains to be checked separately and is not resolved by the classification analysis above: because the reply feature generates synthetic text, the generative-output transparency duties in Article 50 should be assessed on their own terms, since they apply irrespective of risk class. Article 4 AI literacy likewise applies to the operator and to the operator's deployers regardless of the system being minimal-risk.

Yes, inferring religious or philosophical beliefs and political opinions from biometric data is a prohibited AI practice, not merely a high-risk one. Article 5(1)(g) prohibits the placing on the market, the putting into service for this specific purpose, or the use of biometric categorisation systems that categorise individually natural persons based on their biometric data to deduce or infer their race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation. Marketing and ad targeting is not carved out: the only limits on that prohibition are that it does not cover labelling or filtering of lawfully acquired biometric datasets, such as images, based on biometric data, and categorising of biometric data in the area of law enforcement. A commercial ad-targeting system that individually categorises users by faces, voices or other biometric data to infer their religion or political views falls squarely inside the prohibition, and no risk-management, transparency or conformity measure can cure it, the practice must not be placed on the market, put into service for that purpose, or used at all. The high-risk analysis is therefore subordinate but worth stating for the remainder of the operator's system. Biometric categorisation according to sensitive or protected attributes or characteristics based on the inference of those attributes is listed in point 1(b) of Annex III, so under Article 6(2) any biometric categorisation function that survives for example inference of non-prohibited attributes, is high-risk. The Article 6(3) derogation is unavailable to you: it applies only where the system performs a narrow procedural task, improves the result of a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment, or performs a preparatory task, and in any event it never applies where the system performs profiling of natural persons, which is precisely what interest-based ad targeting does. A provider concluding non-high-risk status must document that assessment before placing the system on the market (Article 6(4)) and remains subject to registration under Article 49(2); a high-risk Annex III(1) system must be registered in the EU database before placing on the market or putting into service (Article 49(1)). By contrast, grouping users solely by their stated interests, without processing biometric data, engages neither Article 5(1)(g) nor point 1(b) of Annex III, since both provisions are anchored on categorisation based on biometric data. The decisive line is the input: declared preferences, clickstream or purchase history are outside these provisions; facial images, voice or other biometric identifiers used to deduce protected characteristics are inside the prohibition. Note also that Article 5(1)(c) independently prohibits evaluation or classification of persons over a period of time based on social behaviour or known, inferred or predicted personal characteristics where the resulting social score leads to detrimental or unfavourable treatment in social contexts unrelated to those in which the data was originally generated or collected, or to treatment unjustified or disproportionate to the social behaviour or its gravity. For any biometric categorisation the operator's system lawfully retains, deployers must inform the natural persons exposed to it of the operation of that system under Article 50(3), and where the system is high-risk under Annex III(1) the provider must additionally supply instructions for use meeting Article 13(3), including its intended purpose, the declared level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity under Article 15, and any known or foreseeable circumstances that may lead to risks to health, safety or fundamental rights.

Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 as adopted, the version governing this answer, Annex III high-risk obligations apply from 2 August 2026, and nothing in this corpus records any amendment altering that date; a "7 May 2026 Digital Omnibus agreement" is not part of the adopted text supplied, so it cannot be treated as displacing Article 113 here. The mechanism is as follows. A system falls into the Annex III route when it corresponds to one of the lettered use-cases under the eight numbered areas of biometrics; critical infrastructure; education and vocational training; employment, workers' management and access to self-employment; access to and enjoyment of essential private and public services; law enforcement; migration, asylum and border control management; and administration of justice and democratic processes, which Article 6(2) deems high-risk. Article 113(2) sets the general application date of 2 August 2026, and the derogations in Article 113(3) do not touch Article 6(2): point (a) advances only Chapters I and II to 2 February 2025; point (b) advances Chapter III Section 4, Chapter V, Chapter VII, Chapter XII and Article 78 to 2 August 2025, with the exception of Article 101; and point (c) defers only Article 6(1), the Annex I embedded-product route, where the AI system is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment, and its corresponding obligations to 2 August 2027. Because the Annex I deferral is expressly limited to Article 6(1), it gives no relief to an Annex III provider: the full Chapter III Section 2 duty set (risk management, data governance, technical documentation, logging, deployer transparency, human oversight, accuracy and robustness), plus conformity assessment and CE marking, registration, post-market monitoring and serious-incident reporting, bind from 2 August 2026. Two qualifications belong to the same answer. First, classification is not automatic: by derogation under Article 6(3), an Annex III system is not high-risk where it poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing decision-making outcomes, and it performs a narrow procedural task, improves the result of a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the previously completed human assessment absent proper human review, or performs a preparatory task, but it is always high-risk where it performs profiling of natural persons, and the provider must document that assessment before placing the system on the market. Second, obligations already in force are unaffected by the 2026 date: the Article 5 prohibitions and the Article 4 AI-literacy duty on providers and deployers have applied since 2 February 2025 under Article 113(3)(a), and Chapter V GPAI obligations since 2 August 2025 under Article 113(3)(b). Systems placed on the market or put into service before the high-risk obligations bite are governed by the Regulation's separate transitional regime rather than by Article 113 itself, which is why legacy public-authority high-risk systems carry a later compliance horizon.

No. In Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 as adopted, the version governing this assessment, the prohibitions in Article 5 remain applicable from 2 February 2025, and nothing in the adopted text defers that date. The date is fixed by Article 113, which sets entry into force on the twentieth day after publication (Article 113(1)) and general application from 2 August 2026 (Article 113(2)), subject to three derogations in Article 113(3): Chapters I and II, which contain Article 4 (AI literacy) and Article 5 (prohibited practices), apply from 2 February 2025 (Article 113(3)(a)); Chapter III Section 4, Chapter V, Chapter VII and Chapter XII and Article 78 apply from 2 August 2025, with the exception of Article 101 (Article 113(3)(b)); and Article 6(1) with its corresponding obligations applies from 2 August 2027 (Article 113(3)(c)). That list is exhaustive, so the eight prohibited practices in Article 5(1)(a), (h), manipulative or deceptive techniques, exploitation of vulnerabilities by age, disability or social or economic situation, social scoring, criminal-risk profiling, untargeted facial-image scraping, emotion inference at work and in education, biometric categorisation by sensitive attributes, and real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement, have been enforceable since 2 February 2025, together with the conditions attaching to the Article 5(1)(h) exceptions in Article 5(2) to (4) (fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27, EU-database registration under Article 49, prior judicial or independent administrative authorisation with the 24-hour urgency rule, and notification of the market surveillance and data protection authorities). Any subsequent Commission proposal or amending act altering those dates is outside the adopted corpus applied here and cannot be read into Article 113; assessing its effect would require the amended legal version as the governing text.

The Commission's GPAI Guidelines of 18 July 2025 did not introduce a new systemic-risk threshold, they added a separate, lower indicative threshold for scoping: a model is presumed to be a general-purpose AI model when the cumulative training compute exceeds 10^23 FLOP and the model can generate language (text or audio), image or video output. That 10^23 figure goes to whether a model is a GPAI model at all, and therefore whether the Article 53(1) obligations bite, technical documentation per Annex XI (Article 53(1)(a)), downstream-provider information per Annex XII including the subpoints of Article 53(1)(b)(i)-(ii), a copyright policy addressing Article 4(3) rights reservations (Article 53(1)(c)), and a publicly available sufficiently detailed training-content summary on the AI Office template (Article 53(1)(d)). The systemic-risk threshold is unchanged: under Article 51(2) a model is presumed to have high-impact capabilities, and so is classified as a GPAI model with systemic risk under Article 51(1)(a), when cumulative training compute measured in floating-point operations is greater than 10^25, the alternative route being a Commission decision, ex officio or on a qualified alert from the scientific panel, that the model has equivalent capabilities or impact having regard to the Annex XIII criteria (Article 51(1)(b)). Crossing it triggers the Article 55(1) obligations on top of Article 53: state-of-the-art model evaluation including documented adversarial testing (a), assessment and mitigation of Union-level systemic risks and their sources arising from development, placing on the market or use (b), tracking, documenting and reporting serious incidents and corrective measures without undue delay to the AI Office and, as appropriate, national competent authorities (c), and adequate cybersecurity for both the model and its physical infrastructure (d). It also removes the Article 53(2) free and open-source carve-out from points (a) and (b), which by its terms does not apply to GPAI models with systemic risk. Two qualifications matter. First, the Guidelines' 10^23 figure is an interpretive and rebuttable presumption of the Commission's own making; the thresholds in Article 51(1) and (2) can only be amended by delegated act under Article 51(3) in accordance with Article 97, and no such act is reflected in the Regulation as adopted. Second, the Guidelines' one-third rule for fine-tuned or modified models, additional training compute exceeding one third of the base model's compute, or roughly 3.3×10^24 FLOP where base compute is unknown, is likewise guidance on when a modifier becomes a provider, not a statutory threshold; providers may in any event rely on codes of practice under Article 53(4) and Article 55(2) to demonstrate compliance until a harmonised standard is published, and otherwise must show alternative adequate means of compliance for Commission assessment.

Yes, fines can be imposed at EU level, but formally by the Commission, not by the AI Office in its own name and not by national authorities. Article 101(1) empowers the Commission to impose on providers of general-purpose AI models fines not exceeding 3 % of their annual total worldwide turnover in the preceding financial year or EUR 15 000 000, whichever is higher, where it finds the provider acted intentionally or negligently in that it: (a) infringed the relevant provisions of the Regulation; (b) failed to comply with a request for a document or for information pursuant to Article 91, or supplied incorrect, incomplete or misleading information; (c) failed to comply with a measure requested under Article 93; or (d) failed to make available to the Commission access to the general-purpose AI model, or the model with systemic risk, for an evaluation pursuant to Article 92. The AI Office is the Commission structure through which that supervision is exercised, the Commission develops Union expertise and capabilities in AI through the AI Office, and Member States must facilitate the tasks entrusted to it (Article 64(1) and (2)), so the AI Office prepares and conducts the enforcement action while the fining decision is a Commission decision. National authorities have no equivalent power over general-purpose AI model providers. The Member State penalty regime in Article 99 covers infringements by operators, and its 3 % / EUR 15 000 000 tier in Article 99(4) is a closed list, provider obligations under Article 16, authorised-representative obligations under Article 22, importer obligations under Article 23, distributor obligations under Article 24, deployer obligations under Article 26, notified-body requirements and obligations under Article 31, Article 33(1), (3) and (4) or Article 34, and transparency obligations for providers and deployers under which does not include the Article 53 or Article 55 obligations of general-purpose AI model providers. Article 99(3) (prohibited practices under Article 5) and Article 99(5) (incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to notified bodies or national competent authorities) likewise do not reach those obligations. The Article 101 power is bounded by its own safeguards: before adopting a decision the Commission must communicate its preliminary findings to the provider and give it an opportunity to be heard (Article 101(2)); in fixing the amount regard must be had to the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement and to proportionality and appropriateness, taking into account commitments made under Article 93(3) or in codes of practice under Article 56 (Article 101(1)); fines must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive (Article 101(3)); information on fines is communicated to the Board as appropriate (Article 101(4)); the Court of Justice has unlimited jurisdiction to cancel, reduce or increase the fine (Article 101(5)); and the Commission must adopt implementing acts laying down detailed arrangements and procedural safeguards for the proceedings (Article 101(6)). Providers remain separately bound to cooperate as necessary with both the Commission and the national competent authorities in the exercise of their respective competences and powers (Article 53(3)).

No, at 220 employees you have not lost SME status under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, and the Article 62 measures remain available to you. The Regulation does not set its own headcount ceiling; "SME" carries the Union definition (Commission Recommendation 2003/361/EC), whose staff ceiling is fewer than 250 persons employed. Growing from 30 to 220 crosses the micro/small boundaries but stays below the medium-sized ceiling, so the deciding condition is not met by headcount alone. Two qualifications govern whether that conclusion holds. First, the headcount test is cumulative with the financial test: the operator must also stay within an annual turnover not exceeding EUR 50 million or an annual balance-sheet total not exceeding EUR 43 million, and the data must be consolidated with any partner and linked enterprises, if the growth came with a majority investor or a group parent, the operator's consolidated figures, not the operator's standalone 220, decide the status. Second, under the same Union definition a change of status takes effect only where the ceilings are exceeded or fallen below over two consecutive accounting periods, so a single quarter's growth would not in any event flip the status immediately. So long as you qualify, the Article 62 measures retain are: priority access to the AI regulatory sandboxes, conditional on having a registered office or a branch in the Union and on fulfilling the eligibility conditions and selection criteria, that priority not precluding access by other SMEs and start-ups meeting those conditions (Article 62(1)(a)); specific awareness-raising and training activities on the application of the Regulation tailored to SME and start-up needs (Article 62(1)(b)); use of existing and, where appropriate, new dedicated communication channels for advice and replies to queries on implementation, including on sandbox participation (Article 62(1)(c)); facilitated participation in the standardisation development process (Article 62(1)(d)); and, as an SME provider, the taking into account of the operator's specific interests and needs when fees for conformity assessment under Article 43 are set, reduced proportionately to the operator's size, market size and other relevant indicators (Article 62(2)). These are obligations on Member States, not entitlements you self-certify, so expect the national authority to verify the definition against the operator's consolidated accounts. The Article 62(3) actions of the AI Office, standardised templates, the single information platform, communication campaigns and convergence of public procurement best practices, are available to all operators and do not depend on the operator's size at all. The operator's ability to test high-risk AI systems in real-world conditions outside a sandbox under Article 60 is unaffected by the change, because that route is open to any provider or prospective provider of Annex III high-risk systems and is not size-conditioned: it depends on submitting a real-world testing plan to the market surveillance authority and obtaining its approval, with tacit approval after 30 days unless national law excludes it, registration of the testing under Article 71(4) (or in the secure non-public section under Article 49(4), point (d), or under Article 49(5) for the systems specified there), establishment in the Union or an appointed Union legal representative, safeguards for any third-country data transfer, and the remaining conditions in Article 60(4), together with informed consent and free withdrawal by test subjects under Article 60(5), reporting of serious incidents under Article 60(7), notification of suspension, termination and final outcomes under Article 60(8), and liability for damage under Article 60(9).

Not automatically, and not because of the 35% figure: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 as adopted contains no compute-ratio test for when a fine-tuner becomes the provider of the modified general-purpose AI model. Any percentage-of-base-compute threshold circulating in Commission guidance is interpretive and creates no statutory duty, so 35% is legally inert on its own. What decides the question is the ordinary provider concept: the operator is the provider of the fine-tuned model if the operator places that model on the market or put it into service under the operator's own name or trademark, whether for payment or free of charge. On those facts you assume the Article 53(1) duties in respect of the model you have released, (a) drawing up and keeping up to date technical documentation of the model, including its training and testing process and evaluation results, containing at a minimum the Annex XI elements, for provision on request to the AI Office and national competent authorities; (b) drawing up, keeping up to date and making available information and documentation to downstream providers integrating the model, sufficient to (i) let them understand the model's capabilities and limitations and comply with their own obligations and (ii) containing at least the Annex XII elements; (c) putting in place a copyright policy, including identifying and complying with rights reservations expressed under Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790 through state-of-the-art technologies; and (d) publishing a sufficiently detailed summary of the training content per the AI Office template. Article 53(2) disapplies points (a) and (b), but not (c) and (d), where the model is released under a free and open-source licence allowing access, use, modification and distribution with publicly available parameters, unless it is a model with systemic risk. Separately, test classification for the model as you release it: under Article 51(1) it is a model with systemic risk if it has high-impact capabilities (point (a)) or is so designated by Commission decision under Annex XIII criteria (point (b)), with a presumption under Article 51(2) where the cumulative training computation exceeds 10²⁵ floating point operations, a threshold reached on cumulative, not incremental, compute. If it is caught, Article 55(1) adds (a) state-of-the-art model evaluation including documented adversarial testing, (b) assessment and mitigation of Union-level systemic risks, (c) tracking, documenting and reporting serious incidents and corrective measures to the AI Office without undue delay, and (d) adequate cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure. Article 25 is not the route here: it converts a distributor, importer, deployer or third party into a provider only in relation to high-risk AI systems, where they (a) put their name or trademark on a high-risk system already placed on the market or put into service, (b) make a substantial modification to such a system so that it remains high-risk under Article 6, or (c) modify the intended purpose of an AI system, including a general-purpose AI system, not classified as high-risk so that it becomes high-risk. Fine-tuning a general-purpose AI model as such engages none of those limbs.

The operator is both: on these facts the operator is the provider of that system as well as its deployer, not merely a deployer. Provider status turns on developing an AI system and placing it on the market or putting it into service under the operator's own name or trademark; putting into service expressly includes supplying the system for the operator's own use in the Union for its intended purpose. Neither external release, nor supply to a third party, nor payment is a condition, so an HR tool built in-house and switched on for the operator's own workforce is "put into service" by you and you assume the provider obligations. The operator is simultaneously the deployer, because you use the system under the operator's own authority. Article 25 does not help you here: it converts a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party into a provider where they put their name or trademark on a high-risk system, make a substantial modification, or modify the intended purpose, it does not remove provider status from the entity that developed and put the system into service itself. The practical consequence depends on classification. HR uses such as recruitment or selection, decisions on promotion or termination, task allocation, and monitoring or evaluation of workers fall within Annex III, point 4, so absent an applicable derogation the system is high-risk and you owe the full provider set: risk management (Article 9), data and data-governance requirements (Article 10), Annex IV technical documentation drawn up before putting into service and kept up to date (Article 11), automatic logging (Article 12), transparency and instructions for use (Article 13), which the operator must produce even though the operator is the operator's own recipient, human oversight design (Article 14), accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity (Article 15), a quality management system (Article 17), conformity assessment (Article 43), an EU declaration of conformity (Article 47), CE marking (Article 48), registration in the EU database before putting into service (Article 49), post-market monitoring (Article 72) and serious-incident reporting (Article 73). As deployer you additionally owe Article 26: use per the instructions for use with appropriate technical and organisational measures (26(1)); human oversight by competent, trained natural persons with the necessary authority and support (26(2)); input data relevant and sufficiently representative so far as you control it (26(4)); monitoring, and suspension plus notification where a risk or serious incident arises (26(5)); retention of logs under the operator's control for at least six months (26(6)); information to workers' representatives and affected workers before putting the system into use in the workplace (26(7)); and information to affected natural persons where the system is used in decisions concerning them (26(11)). Article 4 AI-literacy duties bind you in both capacities, and Article 50(1) applies only if the system is intended to interact directly with natural persons and this is not obvious to a reasonably well-informed person. No fundamental-rights impact assessment is triggered: Article 27(1) binds only deployers that are bodies governed by public law or private entities providing public services, and deployers of Annex III, points 5(b) and (c) systems. A private employer using an Annex III, point 4 HR system is outside that scope, so the assessment elements in Article 27(1)(a), (f), description of the deployer's processes, the period and frequency of intended use, the categories of persons and groups likely to be affected, the specific risks of harm to them, the implementation of human-oversight measures, and the measures on materialisation of those risks including internal governance and complaint mechanisms, do not apply to the operator unless the operator is a public body or provide public services.
